maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext:
My hon. friend, in moving this motion, desires that we should practically recast the Bill as it has been brought down by the committee, and to set aside the schedule which has been partly agreed upon by the opposition, and partly adopted by the majority. My hon. friend would like to have a new principle adopted. I do not see, however, that the principle which he wants to have adopted can apply to the whole Bill. The proposition which is involved in this amendment is not in itself a principle, but it is simply a proposition to select a certain lot of constituencies for redistribution. If we do that, what will become of other constituencies ? You cannot touch one, still less can you touch five, unless you touch them all, and go over the whole ground. I listened with a great deal of interest to the speech which my hon. friend delivered the other day, and in which, for good reasons which we can appreciate, he showed a good deal of feeling. He spoke eloquently and well in expressing his opinion that the people of Ontario would resent any interference with one of the old landmarks, namely, the county of Norfolk. He made a point which perhaps may appeal to some cf his friends, certainly it appealed to me, for I would like, for my part, to stand by the old historic traditions of this county as much as possible, and to keep them unimpaired as far as we can. But unfortunately, events are stronger than we are in this respect, and notwithstanding our desire and our efforts

to keep these historic traditions unimpaired, we have been forced in the past and we are forced on this occasion, in some measure, to depart from them. But my hon. friend may console himself, and I also take some consolation from the fact, that the county of Norfolk, one of the oldest counties, as he truly stated the other day, is not to disappear. The two ridings of Norfolk will disappear, but those two ridings are comparatively of modern creation. I do not think they date beyond confederation, but I think the old county of Norfolk does date back as far as the early settlement of upper Canada. Therefore 1 rejoice, and my hon. friend will rejoice, that the county of Norfolk is to remain as one of the old landmarks of Canada. But if it required to disappear, there is a precedent for it. The hon. gentleman will remember that there was among the early electoral districts of the province of Ontario an old landmark, still older and more sacred than Norfolk- the town of Niagara, which was closely connected with the early history of Upper Canada. The town of Niagara was one of the constituencies of Ontario at the time of confederation. But the town of Niagara has had to disappear before the necessity of representing advancing population elsewhere. The old constituency of Niagara, which was one of the historic traditions to which my hon. friend referred, even older than the county of Norfolk, has had to disappear. We never hear the name of Niagara spoken now on the floor of the House of Commons as a constituency, though it was a name of frequent recurrence in the early days of confederation, and it was a constituency with which some important members of the Conservative party were associated in those days. It has had to make way before the advancing population of the newer parts of Ontario. Therefore we have had to do some very unpleasant work in this respect, very much to our regret. I may say, and everybody will agree with me, that so far as the province of Ontario is concerned, the present redistribution is one of the most difficult, indeed it is the most difficult that parliament has ever had to deal with since confederation. In 1872 and in 1892 no such unpleasant duty was thrown upon parliament, so far as the province of Ontario was concerned, and no such painful consequences were involved as in this redistribution. In 1872 the representation of Ontario had to be increased, and in 1882 it had still further to be increased In 1892 there was no addition, and I believe there was no subtraction. But, on the present occasion, for the first time since confederation, it has been the duty of parliament to cut off and not to add. Now, my hon. friend will agree1 with me that, in a country like Canada, where population is increasing and being constantly displaced, the work of adding is more agreeable than the work of subtracting, and 358J
not only more agreeable, but much easier. But, on the present occasion, it is the painful duty of the House to remove from the representation of Ontario six of its constituencies. Where was the axe to fall ? The work is an Invidious one, one which cannot be performed without a severe struggle, or without representations beyond number as to which of the constituencies are to be spared, leaving the axe to fall upon tlieil neighbours. I may say that, though I da not belong to the province of Ontario, 1 have had numerous representations mads to me that the axe should fall not upon the constituency of the writer but upon the neighbouring constituency. And, the neighbouring constituency would' at once "be heard from declaring that the axe should tall upon the other. For instance, in this parliament we have the county of Bruce represented by three members, Norfolk by two and Victoria by two. My hon. friend from North Victoria (Mr. Hughes) has, if I may use the expression, kicked pretty vigorously against the idea that the constituency should continue to be represented by only two members. From Bruce we have had representations vehemently protesting against the idea that that constituency should not continue to be represented by three members, and protesting just as vehemently against the idea that its representation should be reduced to two. Now, the county of Middlesex, of which we have heard within the last few days and which has been, selected by hon. gentlemen on the other side as one to which undue favour was shown by this Bill because it is to be represented by three members-, Middlesex is represented at this moment by four members. But we have before ns this painful duty of removing six constituencies from the representation of Ontario, which shall be taken away ? That is the point; that is the trouble. The committee have made representations on this- subject. As I understand, they have agreed upon some suggestions, while they have -differed on some others. If I am correctly informed, the record will show that, so far -as the constituency of Norfolk is concerned, all the gentlemen who composed the committee came to the conclusion that, the representation of Norfolk should be restricted to one member. So far as Victoria is concerned, they did not agree. Now, when we find the committee has agreed with regard to one constituency, I do not think we can do better than they have done. Where they have differed, there is room for debate. I submit to my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Tisdale) that, painful as it is, we cannot do better than accept the unanimous view of the committee. I do hope that, if the hon. gentleman's constituency disappears, we shall not lose his presence in this House. There are other constituencies in Ontario, I hope, that will be glad to avail themselves of his services. They are not all Reformers, in Ontario, I

am sorry to say ; there are a good many Tories left. I hope that one of the Tory constituencies will take my hon. friend as its representative ; for. I must say that, it there are to be Tories from the province ot Ontario I would sooner have my hon. friend than some others. Perhaps he will not take that as a compliment from me ; I do not offer it as such, but simply as an expression of my own opinion.
The consideration of the.motion of my hon. friend and of the principle adopted by this Bill brings me to the point made and strenuously pressed the other day and 1 suppose, to be pressed again-by my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke). That hon. gentleman asked why urban population should not be represented in this House on a par with rural population , Why should there be any distinction between population and population 7 One reason which has been given, and which seems to be one that has force and merit in it-and which. I hope, on consideration will appeal to the sense of fairness of my hon. friend (Mr. Clarke)-is that urban population is, in fact, l'epresented on the floor of this House in greater degree than rural population, owing to the fact that a good many members coming from tlie^ larger centres represent rural constituencies. It is true that there is a more urgent and1* pressing reason, and1 that is that you could not carrv out the idea suggested by my hon. friend. The unit of population for Ontario is about 25,000. You could not apply that unit uniformly to the city of Toronto and the rest of the province, for the effect would be to give about ten members to the city of Toronto, and you would be required to cut off five more rural constituencies. You could not do tbat theie would be a rebellion, almost.

But, if the hon. gentleman thinks there is so much merit in his idea, he can move an amendment declaring that there should be ten members for the city of Toronto. There is another reason. His argument that a man in one part of the country should have equal representation with a man in another part is a purely fallacious one so far as that is concerned. Representation by population, to which my hon. friends on the other side of the House are tardy, very tardy, converts, which, in their day. they fought with all their strength and skill, was never applied in the sense in which it is now suggested it should be applied. Representation by population was simply applied as between the provinces, and originated in the oldi very unwieldy union between Upper and Lower Canada. It did not arise in Upper Canada at first, but in Lower Canada. But when the union took place in 1841, Lower Canada had* a larger population than Upper Canada. Some advanced! Liberals of those days objected to equal representation. Mr. Papineau, In 1S49,* moved that representation by population should be adopted, which would give a greater representation ta Lower Canada than to Upper Canada. The motion was resisted by Mr. Lafontaiue for very good reasons. He would not agree to it without constitutional guarantees in favour of Lower Canada. In the course of time, the balance of population swung to Upper Canada. Then, Mr. Brown took up the cry of 1 Representation by population.' It was fouglit vigorously in those days. Representation was , equalized at confederation, and tlie principle was adopted that, as between province and province there should be an equality of representation based upon population. This principle however never was adopted as a constitutional principle, so far as the representation of one province was concerned. Therefore, the hon. gentleman will find that the principle does not admit of the application he wishes to give it in the representation of his own province. I make bold to say-and it has been shown already-that, in Great Britain and In all parts of the world wherever they have representative institutions, urban population is not given the same voice as is given to rural population. But why 7 My hon. friend will understand the reason at once in a forcible manner as far as the population of the province of Ontario is concerned. Ontario is a growing province. It is extending its sphere jn all directions particularly in the west

and in tlie north. New centres of population are growing up all the time in the north and in the west. There are some already which have grown up and there are others which are starting. The new Canadian Northern railway built along the valley of the Rainy river will take into that district almost a whole province by itself. The new railway which is in contemplation to-day will build up many new communities in the northern and western parts of Ontario. You must provide at once in order to give representation to these communities. One reason why we cannot adopt the principle which has been departed from is this. My hon. friend asked me the question the other day why Lennox and Addington should not be interfered with. Lennox and Addington and Victoria should remain ns they are, because, when we have a new redistribution to make in ten years they will be able to keep their identity while new constituencies will have to be provided with representation in the Rainy River district and other parts of the province.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not propose to detain the committee at
any length in reply to the right hon. gentleman (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) at this time. At a later stage of the proceedings when the motion of which I have given notice and which will have to stand until the third reading of this Bill is taken up, I shall give him his answer to the argument which he has made to-day. I propose, to-day, to confine myself to the task of pointing out one or two matters. I think the right hon. gentleman was unhappy-I would not like to say misleading, but probably I would be entitled to say that-in the illustration he chose in regard to the old town of Niagara losing a member in the House of Commons and in the legislature. The reason why that constituency was wiped out was that it was one of the old boroughs, using the term iu the English sense. There were a few of them in the old times following the English system in Ontario and they have disappeared but not in the manner that I complain of as lessening the representation of Norfolk. It was simply due to a change of system and therefore it would hardly be a parallel for the change in the representation of Norfolk of which I am complaining. It was not so much in one sense that I desired to maintain the' name of Norfolk, though I would like to see it preserved as the right hon. gentleman says truly it is preserved, but my complaint was that the proposed change was lessening the representation of one of the oldest districts in Ontario, because, excepting Niagara town, there is none older than Norfolk. I agree with the right hon. gentleman that redistributions are always difficult even if we try to be fair, and they are especially difficult when, as he points out, there is a reduction instead of an increase in the number of representatives. I pointed out another reason why not only Norfolk but the whole Niagara district should receive consideration. The five counties in the Niagara district in 1892 surrendered two representatives without any great feeling being manifested by either political party. I. myself, as I have explained, on behalf of Norfolk took a load from one of the'adjacent counties showing that when a principle was applied as far as I have been the representative I have never shirked from it. A large township from an adjacent county was put into my riding to equalize the population and to bring it up to the unit. This township has been a Reform township, and it has twice since that time given majorities against me. So that, in addition to the parallel of Niagara not being on all fours with the case of Norfolk, because Norfolk is not an old borough, we had in 1892 two representatives taken from the Niagara district without either party showing any undue feeling about it. because the proposition was fair and the disturbance of other parts of the province of Ontario was avoided by taking out two constituencies and readjusting the

district in such a way that there was no political advantage to either party. One of these constituencies was taken from each side of politics and I think there was no political advantage in regard to either of them. That is one strong reason why we are not now disposed to submit to a further dimunition of representation. You may go too far.
I said nothing the other evening in regard to the political effect of this change. I do not propose to do so to-day. I may at some other time express my opinion in regard to it, hut I am satisfied that when we have such a strong underlying principle that it would be only fair in connection with this Bill or any other Bill that the representation of the Niagara peninsula should not be depleted by one. While I quite agree with the right hon. gentleman that there must be a distinction as between urban and rural population I am still of the opinion that he is not justified in any further diminution of our representation, because, in the previous redistribution of 1892, we gave up two representatives. I do not propose to discuss the principle of this Bill to-day nor do I propose to discuss the effect of it, because, as I will take up some of the time of the House at a later stage in going into the Bill, it would be hardly fair to the House and it is not a desirable thing that I should speak more than once on the same subject, and I am sure that if I did I would speak on the same lines. Therefore, I shall ieave that to a later stage and I will only say that at that later stage I will point out to the right hon. gentleman a method by which the matter could have been satisfactorily settled without any charge or suspicion of any political advantage. The Conservative members in this House, the Conservative party in the country, the independent people and the independent press of Canada, have shown that this Bill is not a fair proposition. Even if it sticks to the principle laid down by the government, it has been shown to be a bad principle. One of the greatest independent papers of the country, has shown that this Bill affects such a change in a political way, that the Prime Minister need not have remarked that self-preservation is the first law of nature. I am quite willing to admit the principle of self-preservation, but I do not want seif-preservation to be so rampant as to absolutely destroy the other fellows. It would be a ridiculous proposition to lay down that they should not lose membership, if they were entitled to lose it by population, simply because they existed before other constituencies, which have now a larger population.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: The Premier said he was going to right the wrong perpetrated In 1882 and if that is his policy, he will have to concede the proposition made by the member for South Norfolk.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext:
If we give the Niagara peninsula two more seats, what would become of Muskoka, Rainy River, Parry Sound and Nipissing ? Shall they be suppressed in order that we can give more representation to the Niagara peninsula ? We have to do either one thing or the other. But even if we agreed to the proposition of the hon. member (Hon. Mr. Tisdale) it still would not satisfy the hon. gentleman from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster). He states that would still be unjust to the Niagara district, which should have three more seats. But if we yielded to my hon. friend from South Norfolk, and gave Norfolk two representatives, he says that would not give justice to the Niagara district. If we are to be hanged, we might as well be hanged for a sheep as for a lamb. If it is not possible to give satisfaction to that section of the country, we
cannot do better. My hon. friend knows that the Niagara district cannot have the representation that it had in 1872, because other districts have come into existence which were not in existence then. The representation of these cannot be provided for unless some representation is taken from some other districts, and that must come from the older parts of Ontario. I sympathize with my hon. friend from Norfolk, who made a strong argument to show that it was really a misfortune and a grievance that the old district of Niagara should be deprived of one of its representatives. But my hon. friend knows that that is the fate of old age. Old age must give way to youth. I am myself reminded of that every day. I am told every day that my health is failing, and that I should take a back seat. Though I am told that every day, I do not think so ; but the time will come when I, like my hon. friend, will have to submit, not only voluntarily, but cheerfully, to the inevitable.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext:
I will tell my hon. friend why there was a compromise in the case of Carleton. It was because after we had accepted, for the purpose of endeavouring to arrive at some agreement, the proposition which my right hon. friend had laid down in introducing this measure, we were told that certain united counties were going to be carved up without regard to their actual county boundaries for the purpose of inflicting a gerrymander on the Conservative party if we did not compromise ; and, having to choose one of two evils, we saw fit to give away our rights in the county of Carleton, because otherwise we w'ere threatened with that gerrymander. We understood that section one of chapter three of the Revised Statutes was to be adopted. Instead of that, afterwards, when it was seen that it would suit the purposes of my right hon. friend somewhat better, we were referred to section three and were told : Stormont, Dundas and Glengarry form a united county ; we will carve it up as we see fit, and give you a dose of some thing you will not like very well. Leeds and Grenville, Northumberland and Durham, Prescott and Russell will be treated in the same way. That was the proposition with which we were threatened, and on account of which we consented to give up our rights, so far as Carleton is concerned. My hon. friend has suggested that this committee- conference, he called it in the first instance; committee he calls it now-was designed to effect and did effect a very fair redistribution. Well, I do not know of one important proposition, so far as the province of Ontario is concerned, emanating from the minority, which was accepted by the majority. I am willing to be corrected if any member of the committee here has a different recollection, but at present I cannot recall one important proposition from the minority which was accepted by the majority of the committee. It was not a conference but simply a partisan committee, upon which were four Liberal members and three Conservatives; and the Liberal members were perfectly frank about it. There were certain matters about which there could not possibly- be any disagreement, but, when we came to places where there could be a little

carving, we soon found out what was the disposition of our lion, friends on the other side. My right lion, friend calls this a conference and has been congratulating himself just now on the fairness of the redistribution. Let me, at the risk of wearying the House, run over the formal proceedings of the committee for a moment. If this were a conference, one would naturally suppose that, to avoid the difficulties referred to by my right hon. friend, arising from pressure from one part of the country or the other, a particular course would have been laid down and certain principles formulated, and the committee would proceed on these, regardless of pressure from any [DOT]quarter. I moved, in the first instance, a series of resolutions, which I think will commend themselves to the judgment of any fair minded man. What were these resolutions ? They were these :
1.	In accordance with the principle laid down by the Prime Minister in the House on the introduction of the Bill, municipal county boundaries shall be observed.
2.	Where separate representation is given to cities the municipal boundaries of such cities shall be observed.
3.	(a.) The municipal county boundaries shall be those set forth in chapter 3, Revised Statutes of Ontario, 1897, and that the word ' county ' herein shall include any provisional county or territorial district established by the said Act.
(b.) The separate representation to he allotted to cities of Ontario shall be first fixed and determined before proceeding with the representation of the rural constituencies.
(e.) The unit of representation for such rural constituencies shall be determined by deducting from the total population of Ontario the combined population of the said cities and by dividing the remainder by the total number of seats to he allotted to rural constituencies.
(d.) The population of any city receiving separate representation shall be excluded in computing the population of the county within which it is situate.
(e.) The redistribution of the representation of Ontario shall then be determined as follows : -
Counties having a population below the unit.
(a.) Each county having a population of not less than two-thirds of the unit shall be entitled to one member.
(b.) Any county not entitled to one member shall be added to that adjoining county to *which it is related as a judicial district, or with which it is connected for judicial or municipal purposes and the representation of such combined counties shall be dealt with upon the principles already and hereinafter stated.
Counties having a population larger than the unit.
(a.) Each county or combined county having a population of not less than 50 per cent and not more than 150 per cent above the unit shall hs entitled to two members, and each county or combined county having a population not less than 150 per cent and not more than 250 per cent above the unit shall be entitled to three members.
(b.) If after applying these principles it i; found that any seats remain to be allotted, such seats shall be allotted to the counties or
combined counties approaching most closely to the conditions which, under the above rule, would entitle them to additional representation.
Division of cities or counties into ridings.
In the division of cities or counties into ridings the geographical limits of each riding shall be as symmetrical and compact as may be possible, always having regard to equalities of population.

The amendment was negatived and the motion agreed to. The amendment of Mr. Haggart was negatived and the motion agreed to. We came next to the county of Perth. The Minister of Public Works moved that it he divided in a certain way. to which Mr. Haggart proposed an amendment. The amendment was negatived and the motion agreed to. Then we come to the county of Northumberland, and the division of that constituency was agreed to, subject to the right to move an amendment at a later date. This amendment was proposed. It was to the effect that this should stand in the list of constituencies returning one member instead of two, and was voted down. Then we came to the county of Essex. My recollection is that the amendment was afterwards moved. And, the question being put upon the amendment, it was declared lost, and the main motion of my hon. friend was declared carried. Mr. Haggart moved that the division should be otherwise. And the question being put upon the amendment, it was declared lost, and the question being put upon the main motion, it was declared carried. But I want my right kon. friend to understand that that is the case because we adopted certain rules, and because, working out those rules, we arrived at practically the same result. My hon. friend opposite has appealed to us on more than one occasion for a little useful information ns to why it is that we on the Liberal side of the House think that we have some justification for making a trifling alteration in the distribution which has prevailed for the last twenty-two years In the province of Ontario, under which distribution I take it upon myself to say that the the province of Ontario, during twenty-two years, has been most vilely misrepresented on the floors of this parliament. Now, Sir, I have here the list of the actual total vote which was cast in the last general election of 1900, and I find that, setting on one side the city of Toronto, the actual results were these : The Liberal party in the eighty-eight constituencies outside of Toronto cast 190,407 votes, and the Conservative party cast 189,777 votes ; with this practical result that the 190,000 vote had 36 of the eighty-eight constituencies, and the 189,000 votes had fifty-two constituencies out of the eighty-eight. Such was the state of things which prevailed at the last general election, such and worse perhaps, because at former elections a very large vote was brought in, as everybody knows, of people who had for a long time ceased to have the slightest interest in Canada or to care one straw what the government of Canada was doing, numbering to my certain knowledge many thousands in the province of Ontario, and many thousands in the other provinces. But, Sir. in 1882, in 1887, in 1891, and in 1896, the practical result of the gerrymander which we are now trying to undo was that the province of Ontario, as I have stated, was utterly misrepresented on the floor of this House. Sir. I say it with knowledge. I say it with the knowledge of those who know anything at all about the practical working of the representation in the parliament of Canada, that the Conservative party were able to retain power in 1S87 and in 1891 Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
solely and wholly by virtue of the gerrymander. Had there been an honest representation in 1887, Sir John A. Macdonald and his party could not have retained power for three months ; in 1891 they would not have retained power for three weeks if there had been an honest representation of the province of Ontario.

I know' the extreme difficulty that there is in carrying out a redistribution of this kiind. I suffered perhaps as no other man in parliament suffered from the tactics pursued in 1882. These were the tactics pursued in 1882. Perhaps the House would like to know; perhaps these gentlemen who now speak about fair play, would like to know how I was treated in 1882. I will tell the House. I had the honour to represent a riding of the county of Huron in 1882. and that county w-as divided by the Conservative distributors in three parts with the intention that I should find it extremely difficult to obtain a nomination. I went up to the county and I had the honour of being unanimously nominated to one of the redistributed ridings, but when I came back to Ottawa, and when they found I

was nominated in spite of their redistribution, then they tore my riding, the riding of centre Huron, into pieces, and they distributed the fragments in such a way that I could not say in which one of the three ridings I had been nominated, and so I had to retire on South Oxford.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: Was that not largely due to the fact that the political friends of the hon. gentleman wished it ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: It is the first time in my parliamentary experience that I have ever heard it so much as suggested, that the Conservative, party paid any regard to any suggestions made by my friends in 1882. I will say this for my hon. friend (Mr. Hughes) that if he had been a member of the House then, his natural sense of fair-play would no dou'bt have revolted against the double injustice which was perpetrated on me. I did not mind the first redistribution of Huron ; that was in the game perhaps and I was willing to take my chances, but the second redistribution was undoubtedly an outrage.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: I sympathized with the right hon. gentleman very much when his own party tried to knife him in South Oxford.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: It so happens that I was not knifed in Oxford, and as the good people of Oxford stood by me I have not much cause to complain after all said and done. I give this as an illustration, because it is right that the House should understand that we haive a serious grievance to redress. I know that many Conservatives at the time, admitted the wrong done in 1882, although it did not prevent them casting their votes against us as a rule. I do say, and I say it advisedly, tlfat if the Conservative party were retained in power in 1887, and again in 1891, it was not due, so far as Ontario is concerned, to the will of the people, but to the gerrymander by which the people were deprived of their right to express their will at the polls. I desire, Sir, that these figures should be placed on record, and that they should remain as a testimony to the position in which we found ourselves when we- were called upon to grapple with this question.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext:
Before the House rose at one o'clock, the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce read a statement which he said he wished particularly to place on record.
I scarcely imagine that any hon. gentleman who listened to that statement could have

very much confidence in it, not because of the hon. gentleman who made it, but because be used figures which be admitted himself were unreliable ; because be excluded the city of Toronto, and be garbled the figures with reference to the cities of Hamilton and Ottawa. That is enough in itself to condemn the statement. Why should the city of Toronto be excluded from any calculation of this kind ? I am going to give a statement with regard to the votes polled under what is called an infamous gerrymander passed by the Liberal-Conservative party in 1882 and the votes polled under the gerrymander passed by the Liberal government of the province of Ontario; and we will see whether there was a gerrymander, and if so in what direction it was. Now, I propose to put on record the facts, not a garbled statement. I propose to give the votes in all the constituencies, with the conditions just as they existed. The Minister of Trade and Commerce excluded West Elgin, North Norfolk, Nipissing and North Waterloo. As everybody knows in West Elgin there were three candidates in 1900 and two in 1896. Therefore, in order to get at the true expression of the people, we have to take the votes polled in 1896 in those four ridings. The total average vote polled for the Conservative candidates was 8,640, and for the Liberal candidates 8,637, a difference of only three votes in the four ridings, which is not material one way or the other. Now, in 1900, in tiie whole province of Ontario there were 56 Conservative members elected by 219, 948 votes, and 36 Liberals by 212,016 votes, or 7,932 less than the Conservative party candidates. I will go further and see whether there was anything like uniformity. The 56 Conservative members who were elected' polled 2,551 as the average vote, and the 36 Liberals who were elected polled 2,502, or 49 on the average less than the Conservatives. The average majority vote polled for the 56 Conservative members was 21,600 ; and the average for the 36 Liberal members was 13,608. The average majority of the Conservative members was 3S6; the average majority of the Liberal members was 380. The defeated candidates polled: the Conservatives, 77,604; the Liberals, 121,929. In the Ontario provincial elections in 1902, upon practically the same lists the Conservatives polled 123,884 votes and! elected 46 members, the Liberals polled 110,375 votes, and elected 4S members; in other words, they elected 48 members as against 46, with 7,034 votes less than the Conservatives. If there is anything wanting to make that practically conclusive in the mind of the right hon. the Premier, it is this, that the Conservatives polled nearly 8,000 votes more than the Liberals in the last election for the whole province of Ontario. The right hon. gentleman shakes his head; but I am stating what is absolutely correct. He points to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who said that he excluded the city of Toronto. Why should he do that ?

speechtext:
The only marked change in public opinion up there is that shown by the vote of the returning officer. The right hon. gentleman has no right to assume that there has been any change of public opinion. There has been some change with regard to the question whether that election was conducted in a very upright manner. There >
are those who believe that it could have

been conducted differently, and that is the only change of public opinion up there. I have given the figures accurately on both sides, and have shown that there is no difference in the four ridings mentioned, except three votes in favour of the Conservative party, and if you take the whole of Ontario-including the city of Toronto, which has just as much right to be included as Kingston and London, which gave Liberal majorities, and the only reason why the Minister of Trade and Commerce excluded Toronto was because it is a Tory citytaking the whole vote in Ontario, we elected fifty-six members as against thirty-six, and we polled 7,932 votes more than our opponents did, and each of our candidates who succeeded had forty-nine votes more than each of the Liberals who were elected. The statement therefore upon which the Minister of Trade and Commerce made so much stress is absolutely worthless and garbled. The right hon. minister admitted himself that he had treated the cities of Hamilton and Ottawa very differently from the others. That is a complete answer to the charge that there was a gerrymander in 1SS2 and another in 1892 which operated to the prejudice of the Liberals. It shows that the Liberal party has in Ontario a majority against it in the whole province, including the city of Toronto. Making the calculations the same in both cases, they have now two more members than the Conservatives, but with a majority against them of something more than 7,000 votes.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: It has been frequently said that figures can be made to prove anything. It just depends on how they are manipulated ; and, given an expert hand at manipulation, you can get them to prove exactly the reverse of what really is the case. My hon. friend contradicts the figures of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Well, I lia\e not the time to go into the columns of figures which my hon. friend has read, but if we can judge of his whole argument by the accuracy of his figures with regard to Nipissing, we will not be disposed to put much faith in it. In 1900 there was an election by acclamation in Nipissing. The candidate was a Liberal who sits in this House, Mr. McCool. I do not think that any one will claim that he is a Conservative. But because he was elected by acclamation, we cannot tell how the people would have voted on one side and the other had there been _a contest. We know how the result would have been in the aggregate, but not the figures on either side. My hon. friend, however, has found an easy way of solving the problem. He takes the election of 1S9G, which was contested by a Liberal and a Conservative, and in wrhicli the Conservative was elected, and he says that the figures on both sides in that election represent accurately the public opinion in that county to-day.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: That only shows that the hon. gentleman's statement, instead of being once wrong, is three times wrong. But the one thing at issue between us is whether there was a gerrymander in 1882. In this connection, I am reminded of what a friend of ours on the other side said in the early part of the debate : Let by-gones be by-gones. That would be my view, but since hon. gentlemen opposite have gone into that old question once more, let me just say that in 1882 the problem was simply to add four members to the province of Ontario ; and in order to do that, the process adopted by the Conservative majority of that day was to carve and manipulate a fraction of no less than fifty-four different constituencies. In order to add a few shingles- to the roof, they took the whole thing down and built it up again. But I can see no advantage in reviving this discussion, because it will not be possible to convince hon. gentlemen opposite. They have laboured so strenuously to try and work themselves into the belief that what was then done was all right-and I suppose if you want to convince others you must first convince yourself-that it would be useless to try and convince them that there was any gerrymander in 1882, or anything but a fair redistribution.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: I understood the right hon. gentleman to differ from the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) with regard to Nipissing, Elgin, Norfolk and AVaterloo. Will he explain how these ought to count ?

speechtext:
No ; because i have not gone into that part of the case at all. I have left it to those who are more expert than I. I do not claim to be an expert in figures, and have been told already that I am not. But I must say that if I were to try my hand at figures, I do not think I could do any worse than hon. gentlemen opposite. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition took the ground that after all we have to-day nothing less than the old system of redistribution. He said we might just as well have resorted to the old way, that we might just as well have prepared the lists and schedules and brought them down to the House instead of having them prepared by a committee. And the reason he gave was that this was a partisan committee. Well, against this assertion of my hon. friend, that there was ao conference, let me point to the fact that, as far as British Columbia is concerned, as he has stated himself, there was no serious difference between the majority and the minority. Let me point also to the further fact that, as regards New Brunswick, the difference was so slight that my hon. friend would not offer an amendment, but reserved his right to do so at a later stage.

In Nova Scotia there was but one discrepancy ; in the territories both sides agreed ; and in the province of Quebec the whole thing was left to the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) on the one side and the Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) on the other. Under such circumstances, will any one tell me that there was no conference, no discussion, no reaching at conclusions ? More than that, as far as the province of Ontario is concerned, we have the statement made on the floor of this House by one of the colleagues of my hon. friend, the hon. member for Lanark' (Hon. Mr. Haggart), that both sides had come to a compromise on no less than five different constituencies-Carleton, Grenville, Leeds and the two Peterboroughs. How does my hon. friend answer that statement ? He answers if, so far as the Peterboroughs are concerned, by saying that his memory is different from that of the hon. member for Lanark.	,

Perhaps it would be reasonable for me to explain my position in reference to the county of Carleton. Under the proposition or plan laid down by the right hon. gentleman, there is not the slightest doubt that the county of Carleton would be entitled to two members. Two of the townships belonging to the county of Carleton under the arrangement have since 1865 belonged to the. county of Russell, that is the townships of Osgoode and Gloucester. They were placed in the county of Russell under the British North America Act. The argument of the supporters of the government who were on the committee was that they ought not to be interfered with. We insisted on our extreme rights that Carleton should have two representatives, and as a compromise the Minister of Justice waived the opinion he had in reference to the division of united counties, that is his objection to dividing them apart from county boundaries, and he gave us a member for the county of Leeds, to which it is doubtful If we were entitled, and got in return two members for Peterborough. We consented to Peterborough, and in that respect I think the hon. gentleman-
That is my hon. friend from Botbwell (Mr. Clancy)-

is mistaken, because the probabilities are that we will carry the two Peterboroughs.
In the face of a concession of that kind which was made by the majority to the minority, we are told that there was no compromise, that no concessions were made in any way to the minority. I understand the case now perfectly. I must say that I expected a little better, but not much. When I proposed the committee, I expected to have a little credit for what was done, but we have received no credit for the concessions that were made to hon. gentlemen on the other side. What they expected was this.
mittee was what it was intended to be, a conference in which the parties gave their views and came to a conclusion ?

Unless they had the power to manipulate the constituency, as they did in 1882 and 1892, they would declare that they were unfairly treated. before in this country in the way of redistribution.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext:
My right lion, friend (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) is still able to congratulate himself on this measure. Well, I am glad of that. He says there was a compromise with respect to live constituencies in Ontario. I cam produce to my right bon. friend the memorandum of the working out of the principle which I placed before the committee, under which Peterborough would have two members. And I repeat that according to my absolute and distinct recollection, there was no compromise so far as Peterborough was concerned. I have the details of the scheme in my room, showing that Peterborough comes under the last section but one of the resolutions which I proposed, and would thus have two members. So far as Leeds and Grenville was concerned, the hon. gentleman says there was a compromise. What was the nature of it ? Was the Conservative proposition accepted ? I believe I read to my right bon. friend this morning the Conservative proposition with regard to Leeds and Grenville and pointed out that it was voted down. All that my right hon. friend has stated with regard to that has no bearing on what 1 said this morning. He does not seem to understand. The compromise with regard to Car let om was that we gave up our right to two members in Carleton on the understanding that counties were not to be taken in groups and constituencies carved out of them regardless of the boundaries of the counties composing those groups. I stated that this morning, and I do not think any hon. member of the committee will differ from me. The case, so far as Carleton is concerned, is exactly as I stated it. The hon. gentleman introduces the constituency of Russell. That was a part of the compromise as to Carleton. For this reason-the two townships which have been part of Russell for some fifty years remain in Russell, this being part of the compromise which includes the giving up of one member in Carleton. There is no such pleasant circumstance as my right hon. friend sees fit to congratulate himself on, that is, there was no real compromise so far as the five constituencies in the province of Ontario were concern ed The compromise from first to last so far as I recollect it-and I think I have a pretty good recollection of it-was this : For the sake of inducing the Liberal members of the committee to abandon the project which they bad in their minds of taking these united counties and carving them up without regard to the county lines within those unions of counties, we accepted the Liberal proposal to sacrifice one member in Carleton and allow the two townships of Carleton to remain in Russell. This is a fact which I stated most distinctly in my remarks
Sir WILFRID LAURI3R.
this morning. And I know of nothing that was accepted on the other side. This proposal with regard to the united counties was put, as I understood it in the shape of a threat, that, unless we consented, every advantage would be taken in the dividing of the united counties.
My right hon. friend has referred to New Brunswick and has said that there was no very great difference there. Does he not know that only one member was to be taken from the representation of New Brunswick ? And, so far as that is concerned, I advocated before the committee a different mode of dealing with it from that proposed by the majority. I did not move a resolution, but reserved my right to move it in the House. In Nova Scotia, two members had to be left out. In the scheme we proposed, the fact was recognized that the county of Pictou must lose one member, a Conservative member. So far as the other member was concerned I advocated and finally moved to have a different arrangement, but I was voted down. That is so far as the province of Nova Scotia is concerned. So far as Manitoba is concerned there was a concession made to us, only one out of many that we asked. The province of Manitoba remains exactly as it was first proposed, as I understand it.

I do no think the Minister of Public Works is stating quite accurately what took place, because I moved my proposition exactly in the same terms as I proposed it at first, on the last day the committee sat, and it was voted

down. So far as British Columbia is cou-cerned, there was very little difference, as my right hon. friend has said, and our proposition was voted down. There was no great difficulty in arriving at an arrangement because the question of the political effect of distributing the ridings was one as to which no one could have the slightest idea. No one knew how it would affect one side or the other. The country was tilling up with population, and In that condition of affairs we had no difficulty in coming to a conclusion. I wish to repeat again, coming back to the province of Ontario, that outside of the compromise with regard to Carleton, I do not think that any proposition from the Conservative side of that committee, of any importance, was accepted by the majority. As I said before, something may have escaped my recollection, I have not had this matter in my mind for five or six weeks, and I will be glad to be corrected if I am mistaken.
Now there was one observation of my right hon. friend this morning that rather astonished me, because I thought I had heard from him language of a different import. I understood him to say this morning that the principle of representation by population had never been adopted by the Liberal party except as between provinces.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: No, I said that it had been so adopted, so far as it applied to provinces. I never disputed that it was not advisable to equalize the representation in the constituencies of each province, but not to make it an absolute principle as between one province and another.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext:
I thought he went a little further than that, and to say that the principle had an application to the provinces themselves. If my right hon. friend will look at his remarks in 1892, at page 3783, of the ' Hansard,' he will find that, speaking as leader of the Liberal party at that time, he enunciated a different principle from that which he advocated this morning, because he said :
There was a pretense of equalizing the population in some of the constituencies, but these weie the exceptions, and the changes made are just as arbitrary as the withdrawal of the change with regard to Clarence. If there is a principle which ought to be recognized in a measure of this kind as far as possible, it is the principle of representation by population. How that principle is to be carried out it is difficult to say.
Now, my right hon. friend was not dealing there

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: Oh, as far as possible. Well, I did not think my right hon. friend was willing to adopt the principle at all. This morning he says it will apply not only to the representation between provinces, but so far as possible he thinks it should apply in the constituencies within a province.
