maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext:
I was somewhat surprised when I heard the remarks of the leader of the opposition with regard to the conduct of business in the committee, because I was under the impression that the greatest possible friendliness and courtesy had existed between the members of that committee, and that we had dealt with the propositions submitted by each side with a great deal of frankness. However, I have often heard it said that when a lawyer has a very poor case the best thing he can do is to abuse the attorney on the other side. Now, my hon. friend this morning, in a very long speech, devoted most of his time to abusing the Minister of Public Works, his colleague on that committee, instead of endeavouring to point out the merits of the respective propositions.
I think if he will read his speech to-morrow he will find that he never attempted, in the case of any of the propositions that were voted down by the majority, to show why it should have been accepted under the rules that had been adopted by the committee. If my hon. friend has reason to feel that the majority of the committee dealt unfairly with him, or that they were mistaken in the conclusions at which they arrived with regard to the delimitation of the boundaries of the various constituencies, it would be far better for him to point out why we were mistaken, wherein we were unfair ; let him compare the propositions that were submitted by the two sides and show wherein the majority of the committee came to a wrong conclusion. My hon. friend complains bitterly that none of the propositions submitted by himself and his colleagues, so far as regards the province of Ontario, were adopted by the majority of the committee. I do not think my hon. friend has any reason for complaining. I have not the same complaint to make with regard to the minority on the committee, because I must say that after conference and deliberation at a great many meetings-this committee sat, I think, something over three months- when he and his colleagues found a great majority of the propositions we submitted to them were fair, they agreed with us and adopted them. I think it would be a more businesslike way for him to point out wherein our propositions were not in ac-

cordance with the rules that we agreed upon to govern the committee.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I am not going to spend any time, because I do not think it is necessary to spend any time, in discussing the conduct of the Conservative party when they were in power, in redistributing the seats in Ontario. If any hon. gentleman thinks there was not a gerrymander in 1882 and in 1892, he is welcome to his opinion.
I am willing to leave that question to the judgment of the people of Canada, and to the historian of those proceedings, to say whether there was not a gerrymander, and a very outrageous gerrymander, perpetrated at that time. It has been pointed out,
I have myself pointed out on a previous occasion, that there was no rule adopted in 1882 and in 1892, requiring that regard should be had to representation by population. The majority of parliament at that time were not handicapped as they are today in considering these questions as they were not as confined to county boundaries, i My non. friend knows that parliament knew when it referred this matter to a committee for consideration, laying down the principle of adherence to county boundaries, that there must be under many conditions great inequalities of population. In that connection I would say" that any comparison with previous acts of this kind would demonstrate beyond question the fairness of the proceedings before the committee. My hon. friend must remember that the meetings of the committee were open to the press, the public and the members of this House, that representations were heard from parties on both sides and that if the majority of the committee had been unfair in any way in respect to one or more of the constituencies we would have' had the condemnation of the press and people of this country. On the other hand I must say that I am pleased to know that the result -of our deliberations has met with the general approval of the people and even of the partisan press with one or two exceptions who support hon. gentlemen opposite. I have noticed some articles in which fault is found with what has been done. I do not spend much time reading the papers but I have found in some of the partisan press that in order to find any ground whatever for criticism they are obliged to wilfully and. deliberately misrepresent the condition of affairs. My right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) ihas referred to a great many of the statements made by the hon. leader of the opposition, but I want to refer to one in particular and that was the statement that he was threatened in the committee with the carving of these constituencies. I must say, that, as far as I am concerned, and I think I speak for the rest of the committee, no such threat existed in the minds of the committee, and I would be very much surprised if my hon. friend could find one word or sentence in the pro-Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND.
ceedings that were taken down that would indicate that a majority of the committee had any such intention or desire or would be guilty of any such proceedings. My hon. friend did, I think, misquote a statement that he said he found in the proceedings of the committee as having been made by me, but it is hardly worth while referring to that because my actions in the committee will speak for themselves.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: If I have misquoted the hon. gentleman I would be very glad to have it corrected now.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext:
1 know my hon. friend probably would not desire to misquote me. In connection with these matters I am not disposed to reply with any feeling to my hon. friend because I know that he has been advised by some of his supporters in regard to these matters and that he has been misled. I know' that if left to himself he never would have formed any such impression. We heard it stated in his absence that a plan had been prepared .^efore the committee met for the redistribution of seats. He has been told these things and perhaps they have made an impression upon him. He has been told that the Conservative members of the committee did not agree with the compromise in regard to Carleton. I am on record as to what I said outside of any informal meetings which I would' not feel at liberty to say much about. We spoke in a very free and frank manner at these informal meetings and perhaps we said a good deal in a joking way. but to take seriously what might be said in a joking manner would be unfair and improper. I have never made any reference to these informal meetings.
I think a. great deal of good was accomplished by sitting down and discussing these matters and trying to arrive at a conclusion that would be fair to both parties. My hon. friend must have been informed by some person else that the committee would be guilty of some such action as that which he ascribes to it. I want to make a reference, and I want to do it in as mild language as I can, to the complaint which my hon. friend makes because the proposition in full was not adopted by the committee. That is where I think he misquoted me, or if he did not misquote me, he misrepresented my position in regard to it by only quoting part of what I said. His friends cheered and in this way tried to put a meaning on what I said that was never intended. If my hon. friend will look at the proceedings he wRl find that I said, and the majority of the committee agreed with me, that as far as the principle of county boundaries was concerned we felt it our duty to adhere to that principle and that if it were departed from in any particular it must be done by a unanimous agreement between the parties. I think my hon. friend will find on record

tlae fact that that is what governed our action and that if we did make a change it was because it was agreeable all round. I do not think my hon. friend's complaint as to the action of the majority of the committee is well founded. Whenever my hon. friend made a suggestion or presented a proposition which was suggested to him, of which he could not have the same personal knowledge as his friends and supporters from Ontario, he was always given an opportunity for consultation and the committee was adjourned on many occasions for that purpose. Then, at the last, when he_ said that he wished to consult some of his friends from Ontario in regard to the propositions which have been carried by the majority, and itbat he was not prepared at the moment to make the amendment that he wished to make, the majority of the committee, instead of sticking to the rules that generally govern bodies of that kind, were perfectly agreeable that these amendments, after consultation with his friends, should be submitted and considered in Committee of the Whole House as we are now considering them. What do I find when I examine these amendments ? I find that after careful consideration and consultation with his own supporters from Ontario, five amendments proposed by him are exactly the propositions the hon gentlemen opposite are condemning as unreasonable and as partisan, and which were made by myself as a member of the committee. My hon. friend must know that there must be some mode of procedure and I do not think my hon. friend will find fault with me as a member of the committee for making propositions when he and his friends offer propositions which in general instances are exactly the same. I made these propositions as a member of the committee after hearing the evidence, and the committee after consideration, adopted them. I findi that five of them which were proclaimed in a general way to be outrageous propositions are exactly the same as those which my hon. friend now proposes. There cannot be anything particularly outrageous from a party standpoint in these propositions when we find that after consultation hon. gentlemen opposite are perfectly agreeable to adopt them. My hon. friend wants to convey the idea and it is more by insinuation and innuendo than by direct statement that he blamed the majority of the committee and myself for having made these propositions. I 'moved as a member of the committee certain propositions in regard to Russell, Brant, Perth, and so on. I dare say the onus in a way fell upon the majority of the committee to make these propositions.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman what five propositions are the same ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext:
I find by reference to the amendment, and I have not examined the list very carefully,
that Algoma is set down to be divided according to the proposal moved by Mr. Sutherland. The fact that my name appears is a matter of form because some members of the committee had to take action.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: But there was no amendment made in that case.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: I do not find any amendment made, but my hon. friend and his followers have been! stating in a general way that a gerrymander is being attempted, and my hon. friend gave this morning an impression that he had a grievance against me because I moved the proposition, because it was carried by a majority of the committee and because the amendment made at that time was not adopted. My hon. friend said that he wished time to consider some of these propositions. He lis considering them. These suggested amendments really should not appear as amendments because they are the same in several instances as the ipropositions adopted by the committee. Then, there are Peterboro, Oxford, Renfrew, Wellington and York. That makes six instead of five. These amendments are ex-[DOT]actl'y the same as I proposed in the committee. Instead of wasting time in discussing general propositions as to what took place in 1882, and 1892, and in the committee this session, let us get down to business and compare the propositions made by the two parties, and see whether the majority were not warranted on every ground of justice and fair-play, in refusing the propositions submitted by the Conservative members of that committee ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman refer to the propositions that were submitted to the committee, outside of these included iu the Bill ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: The Bill, as finally adopted, was carried by the majority of the committee, and it, of course, represents their views.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: The hon. gentleman does not undertake to say that certain propositions made by members of the opposition are the same as certain propositions made by the majority of the committee that were not adopted and are not in the Bill.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: I am pointing out that after consultation and consideration, the opposition adopted most of the propositions in this. Bill, and especially six of them.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: As they are in the Bill ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext:
Yes. It is only fair to say that many propositions were made to the committee, and while they do not formally appear as having been adopted by either the majority or the minority, yet we agreed after consultation

1140$
as to what we would do with regard to them. Therefore, a great many of the propositions as set forth in this Bill were perfectly satisfactory to both parties, and I merely moved them as representing the majority. I regret that the leader of the opposition should insinuate that he was unfairly treated, or that there was any partisanship displayed by the majority of the committee. We appeal to the majority of this House, and we appeal to the people of the country to say whether-taking the propositions of the minority and the propositions of the 'majority-the propositions of the majority were not fairer under all circumstances, than the amendments submitted by the minority. No matter how many figures you may produce, or how much time you may take up discussing this matter, in the end the people of Canada, and especially the people of the particular counties interested in the changes, will have to say whether any injustice has been done. My hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) cited the county of Perth to show that some partisanship influenced myself or my colleagues. The fact is that the minority submitted one amendment, and after consultation, they submitted another amendment, and I take the responsibility before the House and before the electors of Perth of saying that the majority proposition, as contained in this Bill, is the fairer proposition of the two. And so with regard to Simcoe. My hon. friend from Simeoe (Mr. Bennett) appeared before the committee and made a suggestion, and T can with confidence appeal to the electors of that constituency to say that the proposal in this Bill is fairer than the one he suggested. I think the leader of the opposition and his colleagues on the committee will concede that. The hon. member for East Simcoe did not seem to attach much importance to it anyway, and I think at one stage he offered to flip a copper as to whether a certain township should go into his riding or not.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: That was when I found you had such a fixed opinion against me.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: I do not think that any one, on the committee believes that the hon. gentleman had made out a good case for his proposition.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: I would be obliged to you if you will now make the change that I suggested.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext:
We can easily show that the proposition of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) is not as fair as that contained in the Bill. As to the county of Lambton, the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) appeared before the committee, and if my memory serves me, his only suggestion was to change one village from the east to the west, and I believe he admitted that no political significance attached to it one way or the other. In many of these counties with respect to which am-Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND.
endments were moved, the difference between us was very material.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: But you stuck to your own proposition all the time.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: I stuck to it,because I thought it was fair, and just, and proper, and I am prepared to prove it. Let us take Huron and Lanark, and even the city of Toronto, and see what was done with respect to these constituencies.	,

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: Do we not have to take them up one by one ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: Let us discuss them on their merits.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: Why are you talking so long ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: I am talking because the leader of the opposition sought to convey an unfair impression with regard to the action of the committee. He found fault because the rules he suggested, some considerable time after the committee had been sitting, were not agreed to. These rules have been suggested to him, no doubt, and after he- knew how they would work out, I do not think the hon. gentleman insisted on our adopting them. Practically all of the important ones [DOT] amongst these rules had been adopted by the committee to the fullest extent. I do not know exactly what to say about the action of the minority in this matter, but I do not think that the leader of the opposition, being a professional man of high standing, and having a high position in this House would attempt to play a small trick upon his colleagues in the committee. However, when you notice one of the little rules that was worked into this proposition, you will see that it affected only one riding in the whole province of Ontario. The effect of that, if it had been adopted, was to give a party advantage to the Conservative party; but I do not think it would have been right to have adopted it.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: What rule was that ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: That was when my hon. friend wanted to add to the principle of county boundaries which was set down by parliament to guide the committee, the principle that judicial boundaries should be recognized, but only in the case of counties having less than 'the unit of population.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: The hon. leader of the opposition wanted chapter three of the Revised Statutes of Ontario to be taken as a basis.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext:
No. There was some difference of opinion as to what would be the legal effect of the chapter of the Ontario Statutes to which my hon. friend refers. After full discussion

of tliat with the legal fraternity, it was decided by the committee to refer the matter to the Department of Justice. Instead of a majority of the committee attempting to regard a union of counties as one county, which they could do without disregarding the principle which had been laid down by this House, and to which the hon. leader of the opposition himself had given countenance, by submitting it in writing as a principle that should govern the committee; the best proof I can give to this House that the majority of the committee had no such intention is that they made no such proposition. Several weeks previous to this proposition having been made by the leader of the opposition, I had submitted to him what was in my opinion as a member of the committee a fair distribution amongst the several counties, without reference to the question whether they were municipal counties under the Act or not-taking them geographically as they appeared, and as they had previously been represented in this House. There could be no clearer proof that we never at any time intended or desired to change the rule that was governing the committee, where it could be applied with any equalizing of the population. As the Premier to-day pointed out, the committee had very great difficulties, more than any other party had before in trying to arrange properly the representation in this House. The very fact that we had to lose six members in the province of Ontario made it very much more difficult, and perhaps created some feeling in localities where there would otherwise have been no cause for its existence. Every fair-minded man must realize that there was a difficulty; and instead of bon. gentlemen finding fault with the action of the committee, I would like them to point out how they could have done better, or what rule they could have adopted that would have worked more fairly than the rule adopted by the committee.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: Has not that been pointed out time and again ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: No, I do not think it has been, nor do I think, that any effort has been made to show what rule should have governed the committee, that would have worked out better than the rule we adopted.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext:
Will the bon. gentleman permit me to ask him a question ? Will he tell the Committee why he adopted the municipal county boundaries as laid down in the draft which he said was proposed by the leader of the opposition as a fair distribution ; and afterwards, when he found that the rule proposed by the hon. leader of the opposition did not work out to suit him and his friends, he receded from that position, and proposed to unite the counties? Will he tell us why he gave Middlesex three members at the outset without consulting
anybody, and why he gave Northumberland two ? And yet he and his friends sat down to prepare that schedule as it is today, as a fair arrangement, and in doing so violated every rule or decency that should govern a committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: I say it did violate every rule of decency.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: An lion, gentleman has no right to say that another bon. member acted indecently.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: I did not say so. I said that every rule of decency was violated, and I adhere to the statement. The lion. Minister of Public Works, knowing perfectly well what the unit was, stated that the city of Toronto had been excluded. The whole thing had been figured up and calculated by his friends. Perhaps I had better read it to the hon. gentleman. *

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: I am constrained to interfere here. I am going to ask the Committee to be good enough to come back to the question that we ought to to be discussing. We have now spent four hours, and I cannot say that the Committee have been in order fifteen minutes during those four hours. They have discussed almost every question other than the one before the Committee. I am forced at this stage to call the attention of the Committee to the fact that the question now under discussion is the question of connecting the county of Norfolk into one riding, to return one member. This does not involve the principle of the division of county boundaries at all, but involves the acceptance of the county boundaries as they are described on the map. Therefore this discussion is wholly out of order. We have made no progress to-day after four hours of weary sitting. When the question of the division of Middlesex and the other counties which are to have two or more ridings comes up, these questions wifi be in order. I appeal to the Committee to assist me in keeping that order which is absolutely necessary if we wish to make any progress, and get home before the snow flies.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: Will you read the resolution ?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: That the county of Norfolk shall form an electoral district, to be called the electoral district of Norfolk, and shall return one member.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: Read the amendment.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: The amendment is out of .order. If I am asked to put it, I shall give my reasons for declaring it out of order.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: I have listened, Mr. Chairman, with great respect to your ruling, but I am inclined to believe that I am still in order.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: The hon. gentleman may be in order, but when he interrupted me to ask a question, he is hardly in order in going on to make a speech. He will have an opportunity of explaining his views to the Committee when I am through. It is a matter of supreme indifference to me whether the hon. member for Botliwell (Mr. Clancy) thinks I acted indecently on that committee or not.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: I diiT not say that the hon. gentleman did act indecently. It was Mr. Chairman who applied that term.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman thinks that in submitting that memorandum to my colleagues and the committee I did what was not right, he and I differ very much.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: I did not say, that.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: I have already explained how that came to be submitted to the committee. The hon. gentleman thought he had some reason for attacking the Liberal party w'hen he made the statement, which is without foundation, that that memorandum was prepared by a Liberal committee representing the Liberal party in Ontario. But after inquiring into the matter and finding my statement to be correct, that no Liberal committee had anything to do with it, he has taken another means to try and show that there was something improper in the submission of that memorandum, because its recommendations are very much the same as the provisions in the Bill.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: Wait until I read it all.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is at perfect liberty to read it all. There were several meetings of the committee previous to the submitting of that memorandum.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: Informal

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: I am not going to make any reference except to what is right and proper. There were some formal and some informal meetings.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: There was no formal meeting at which any business was done before that.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext:
I accept my hon. friend's statement. There may not have been any conclusion arrived at, but there were formal meetings and the procedure was discussed. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition asked me one day what my views were with regard to the redistribution in Ontario, and I explained them in a general way. I had no memorandum and there was no one present. I explained to my hon. friend, in a general way, just looking at the map. how the constituencies might be redistributed. At his request, I had my views put in writing after-Mr. CLANCY.
wards. My hon. friend must have seen the memorandum afterwards.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: What memorandum ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: The memorandum pointing out how many constituencies I thought might be entitled to one, how many to two, and how many to three members, and what counties vhere were. I never professed to be ignorant of the conditions of my province. I have some knowledge of them, and was willing that my colleagues in the committee should have the benefit of my advice. I do not think there Is anything in that memorandum suggesting how these delimitations were to be made within the counties, and I do not believe he will find any such suggestions in any of the papers which, he says, were submitted to the leader of the opposition. However, whether at a formal or informal meeting, there was nothing done which was improper and of which I have any reason to be ashamed. I did all I could to facilitate' the business of the committee, and I do not believe that the leader of the opposition or his colleagues will say that I was not perfectly frank, or that I did not give every information within my possession and discuss every matter, whether party politics or otherwise, in the freest possible way. If my views were placed in typewriting for the consideration of the members of the committee, it was in order that the leader of the opposition, not being familiar with the province of Ontario, might have an opportunity of submitting to his friends and colleagues what, in a general way, would be the views of the majority of the committee. There was nothing binding in that.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has made it binding since.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: It shows, so far as I was personally concerned, that we were willing to deal with these matters fairly, as they have been dealt with by the committee. And the minority on the committee accepted, with a few exceptions, what was done. It appears to me that the members of Ontario have at present two great grievances. First, that with regard to seme half dozen constituencies, and that is the maximum

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: There are more than thirty involved.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is even far more partisan than I thought he was. If the constituencies could be adjusted to suit him, he would have nothing to say ; but as he cannot have them divided so as to work great unfairness to the Liberal party, he is dissatisfied. He cannot lay his finger on any change that is not perfectly defensible.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: What about Middlesex ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: That will be discussed on its merits when we come to it..	.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: The hon. gentleman can discuss it now.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: No, he cannot.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext:
I understood that by agreement, the amendment of the hon. member for South Norfolk (Hon. Mr. Tisdale) was moved and the general question and everything could be discussed.
I do not intend to occupy the time of the Committee much longer, but I felt called upon to make some observations in view of the statements of the leader of the opposition. I have never held the leader of the opposition and his colleagues responsible for the unreasonable and indefensible propositions which have been submitted in this House. They only show how unfair some of the supporters of the hon. gentleman would be if they had a majority on the Committee. It only goes to show that if they had the power which they had in 1882 and 1S92, they would be quite willing to promote the same unfair dealings in these matters as they did then. My proposition is then, that having covered the two or three points, I think that ought to be satisfactory. And, where a difference exists between us, I think the remarks of my hon. friend from South Lanark, which have been read, show that he believed that, in making the compromise on departing from the principle of county bounds his side had gained a partisan advantage. At any rate, it is clear that in at least two constituencies it would be of advantage to the Conservative party. How then, does it lie in the months of hon. gentlemen opposite to accuse the majority of partisan action or of endeavouring to take a party advantage ? The facts themselves disprove it. and it is acknowledged in the speech of the hon. member for South Lanark. His statement disproves that there was any such action, or that it will have any such effect. Where we departed in one particular from the rule, it was for the reasons given already on which we are all agreed. I should hope that, instead of wasting time in referring to gerrymanders of past decades, instead of speaking in a general way of what took place and what did not take place-for we And things alleged here that did not take place-we shall get to work, as you 'Mr. Chairman suggest, and discuss these propositions and the amendments to them. Then it will be for the majority to say whether the majority of the Committee shall be upheld or whether the contentions of the minority deserve consideration.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman-

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext:
Before the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) begins, I would like to say a word. The Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) has given an extended explanation of what took place in the Committee. And, as the hon. leader of the opposition was a member of that Committee also, I think he should have the right to answer. But after that hon. gentleman has finished his speech,
I am going to ask the Committee to confine itself to the question we are discussing.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: Perhaps it would be better as the point of order has been raised, that we should understand where we are. This morning we took up the amendment of my hon. friend from South Norfolk (Hon. Mr. Tisdale). I had to state to my hon. friend that his amendment had been ruled out of order. I stated then and there that, since my hon. friend wanted to have a vote, if agreeable to him he might move his motion as a substantive motion, in order to have this further discussion on the merits of the Bill, and to be fair to both sides, I think that proposition was placed before the Chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: The proposition placed before the Committee by the hon. member for South Norfolk, is much larger than the point on which we had the discussion which took place to-day. And I simply allowed it to remain before the Committee. I am strongly impressed with the idea that it is my duty as Chairman, to see to it that nothing is placed before the Committee except what is right and proper under the rule. I would have ruled this out of order, but I submitted to the right hon. leader of the House, who in his magnanimity desired that a general discussion of the matter be allowed. We have spent nearly four hours in the discussion of this matter, and, at the end, I only ask the Com-, mittee to decide upon the matter and let us proceed with something else.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: Am I to understand that, after four hours of discussion, you rule the motion before the Chair out of order

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: No.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: Then, I do not quite understand

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) was not present when the motion was placed before the Committee. 1 ruled it out of order. But the right hon. leader of the government said this afternoon that it would be his desire and wish to allow this to remain before the Committee, to give the Committee greater latitude in the discussion than they would otherwise have.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: My hon. friend from South Norfolk (Hon. Mr. Tisdale) said he wanted to have his motion decided by the House. So I agreed to have it left before the House to have it voted upon.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: It must be a question before the House and must be opein for discussion. And, when an effort was made to curtail or rather limit the discussion, I asked that the motion be read; and then, for the first time the original motion was read, and the amendment which, I understood, was before the House was not read at all. But now we are told this is out of order.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: The Chairman ruled that it was out of order as an amendment. And I agree with him. But, out of deference to the wish expressed by the hon. member for South Norfolk, as he wishes to test the opinion of the House, I agreed to take the motion as a substantive motion. But now the Chairman thinks that we have had, perhaps, enough discussion to cover the ground, and I agree with him.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: So long as this is before the Chair, it must be discussable, and we cannot be curtailed of our rights in the discussion of anything before the Chair.

speechtext: This is a motion with respect to which the Committee have no rights. But an agreement was arrived at that the sense of the Committee should be taken on this question. The Committee have no right to claim this from the Chairman as an amendment, because it is not really an amendment. Many reasons could be given, if necessary, why it is not in order.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: There may be a little difficulty, under your ruling, Mr. Chairman, in dealing with that question, because, strictly speaking, in voting upon it, we are not voting as members of parliament, but somewhat in the guise of arbitrators. However, that can be arranged afterwards. I desire to say a word or two with reference to the statement of the hon. Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Sutherland). That hon. gentleman reproached me for making a long speech-of which I had not been aware-and then he occupied with his speech three times as long as I occupied with mine. I must say I thought it was hardly necessary. I was particularly pained by the accusation on the part of the hon. minister that I had abused him. If there is one thing I endeavour to be particular about, it is not to abuse anybody. If my hon. friend will point out the abusive language that I used, I will withdraw it. I will resume my seat to give the hon. gentleman the opportunity to do so. I am afraid the hon. gentleman will find it difficult

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,

speechtext:

The question being put upon the motion, it was negatived, Messrs. Borden and Haggart voting for it, and Messrs. Fitzpatrick, Sutherland and Davis voting against it.
My hon. friend may have thought I was reading from the typewritten report. I was not, I was reading from the resolution. In the first place, I was reading from the resolution which I proposed ; my hon. friend asked me a question as to the disposition of it, and I read what immediately followed, without cutting off or leaving out anything.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: I may have misunderstood my hon. friend. I thought he said I was not willing to adopt the principle of adhering to county boundaries, and quoted something from the proceedings to that effect. I think the proceedings will show, on the contrary, as I stated as explicitly as I could, that I would not as a member of that committee depart from the principle of county boundaries unless it were in some eases we were discussing, and by unanimous consent.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: My hon. friend misunderstood me, because I was talking about this resolution as a whole, and I said what I think he will remember himself, that he did not find any particular objection to that, but he said he did not know exactly where we would be, or something of that kind, if we adopted that. That is perfectly accurate, is it not ? Surely my hon. friend does not suggest that is abuse ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: I would be only too glad to know that I had misunderstood the hon. gentleman.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext:
If I am stating things that are perfectly accurate, my hon. friend cannot suggest that I am in the wrong. Then I went over a number of the

resolutions, and I read exactly wliat I found in the report. Surely my hon. friend does not regard that as abuse. I was not attaching any particular importance to the fact that he moved these resolutions. My hon. friend from Lanark moved the amendments In every case, being the member of the committee from the province of Ontario representing the minority. My hon. friend being upon the committee as the only Ontario member outside of the chairman, naturally had to make these motions. I was not attaching any importance to that. I was merely reading the record, and surely my hon. friend does not suggest that rending- the record was any abuse of him. My hon. friend knows the way in which I gave thb illustration. maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: 1 will take it back, for I did not intend it in that sense at all.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: Now, my hon friend did, I think, abuse me a little, but I am not going to resent it at all. He accused me several times of being unfair. All I can say is that I was not deliberately unfair. If he is of the opinion that I was unfair-I do not know whether he is of the opinion that I was deliberately unfair-but he has accused me of being unfair in wanting certain propositions put before the committee. He will pardon me if I venture to say that that sounds much more like abuse than anything I said.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext: No, I said I did not think the hon. gentleman was responsible.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS,
speechtext:
So far as that is concerned, I think that I can part company with my hon. friend with a very clear conscience. Now my hon. friend also says that there were perfectly friendly and courteous relations between the members of the committee. That is absolutely true, we were friendly and courteous towards each other-at least, I endeavoured to be so, and my Ihon. friends on the other side were always so to me. My hon. friend says they were frank. I admit again that they were frank. They were not only friendly, and courteous, and frank, but they were very firm. That is what I am criticising more particularly. It was done in a very nice manner, there was no discourtesy. My hon. friends on the other side acted like perfect gentlemen in dealing with this matter, so far as the ordinary amenities of everyday life were concerned, but all the same 'they were very firm about it. I do not know that the friendly relations, the courtesy, the frankness, and so forth, relieved the situation very much so far as the delimitation of the boundaries was concerned.
Now, my hon. friend several times during
the course of his speech suggested that we should leave this discussion and get down to business. I should be very glad indeed to see that done. My hon. friend went on something like three-quarters of an hour after lie suggested that. But nevertheless we will have to come to business some time, and then we will be able to consider these matters in more detail. So far as adjournments and everything of that kind were concerned, we got all the courtesy that we asked for. Whenever it was convenient to the other side that there should be an adjournment, we always consented, and all these matters went as they should go, even in a partisan committee. But the point is that his was not different from any ordinary committee that is struck in this House. It was not a conference, it was a committee, one on which one side had a majority and the other side a minority.
My hon. friend attached a great deal of importance to the fact that in certain amendments which I proposed on the last day of the proceedings he found that in six' instances the delimitation was the same as the amendments proposed. Has my hon. friend forgotten that those delimitations related to eighteen counties, each having two ridings, and to five counties divided into three constituencies each, making in all fifty-one ridings ? So, along with the city of Toronto, you have fifty-six ridings, out of which my hon. friend is able to point out we agreed to the delimitation in six. I am inclined to think he is a little under the mark, I think there may have been one or two more than six. But say there are six or eight upon which we agreed out of the fifty-six. He must see there was a great difference of opinion in respect to the delimitation of those constituencies which were divided into more than one riding. Now, I do not know that after this long discussion that has taken place that it is of any advantage for me to prolong it. I agree with what the Minister of Public Works has said that we will be able to discuss these matters a little more directly when we come to the counties in respect of which there has unfortunately been a great difference of opinion in the committee.

Liberals had decided upon a plan, and from that day to this they have not changed their plan, and that plan is embodied in this Bill without the slightest variation. That Liberal plan was decided on before there was a committee at all, before there was a single man on either side of the House heard ; it was a cut and dried plan as to what the Liberals would do, and it is exactly what they did. Surely the Prime Minister cannot call it a conference, when his own friends had already decided that a certain Bill should be submitted1, and when they have insisted in their intention so that the Bill we have now before us presents no variation from the decision they arrived at before they went to the committee. It is nonsense to say that this Bill is a compromise. It is a mere registering of the conclusion come to by the Liberals before hand. I do not know of anything more damning, metaphorically speaking, than the statement that was made by the Liberal party before entering this committee.

We have heard a good deal in this discussion about the fairness of the redistribution. The right hon. the Prime Minister, when introducing the Bill, promised us a fair redistribution, and I believe he intended keeping his pledge, but I cannot believe that either he or the committee fully understand the conditions of the county of Victoria and the provisional county of Haliburton, or they would not have formed them into one constituency as they have done by this Bill. The Minister of Public Works said this afternoon that this redistribution was so fair that even the Conservative newspapers were quoting it as a fair one. I do not desire to quote from newspapers, but I shall cite an article in the Toronto ' News ' on this very proposition :
The government's procedure in the case of Victoria is based upon what cannot be called anything better than a pretext. It involves treating Haliburton, which is a provisional district, having some four thousand population, as a negligible quantity, which can be tacked on to anything. Victoria and Haliburton are not united counties. If they were there would be no possible excuse for not giving them two members. But the population of Victoria aloae is just insufficient to give it more than one member. The one member has, therefore, been allotted to it, and then Haliburton has been thrown into the constituency, as one would throw a single township or a border village, without its claim to proportional representation being ever considered at all. 'You would not have it in Hastings, so we put it into Victoria,' is all the defence or explanation that is offered.
That is an exact exposure of the condition of things, and better stated than I could state it. The argument of the Minister of Public Works is that we talk about Victoria county as a county, while Haliburton is not a county. Therefore, [DOT] because Victoria is not quite enough population for two members they give it one, and then they throw in Haliburton, and because Haliburton is not a county, it does not count. That is a most preposterous position to assume. I can tell hon. gentlemen opposite that in the county where I live the friends of hon. gentlemen opposite are opposed to this arrangement, and look upon it as an outrage. I do not know, hut I think the government have heard! from those people up there. They say there is no sense in this proposal. No party can undertake to put up a candidate there unless he is a millionaire

But the amendment of my hon. friend would have the effect of adding one to the eighty-six members provided for in this Bill. If we carry this amendment and give Victoria two members, we have that painful task before us from which my hon. friend has shrunk-we must strangle somebody. Whom shall it be-Peterborough, Lanark, Northumberland, Middlesex, Toronto ? If my hon. friend will agree with his neighbour (Mr. Clarke) to have one representative less given to Toronto, I have no objection. Somebody must make the sacrifice, and if there is somebody disinterested enough

'Mr. VROOMAN. Take Middlesex.

'Mr. VROOMAN. What about what is right in the matter ?

speechtext: I do rot know that there is anything wrong. Six constituencies in Ontario must disappear. There is the difficulty which hon. gentlemen opposite will not see. maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext:
Surely the appeal made by my hon. friend from South Victoria (Mr. Vrooman)^ -will not fall upon deaf ears so far as the right hon. Prime Minister is concerned, particularly in view of the solicitude that right hon. gentleman has expressed for the due representation of the outlying portions of the province of Ontario. The hon. member (Mr. Vrooman) has presented a map showing the enormous extent of territory covered by the provisional county of Hallburton and the size of this constituency of Victoria and Haliburton as compared Mr. VROOMAN.
with the constituencies to the south. If there Is anything in the argument that urban constituencies should be despoiled of their rights in order that these outlying, sparsely settled districts may be given representation larger than that given the rest of the province, surely the right hon. gentleman, having the authority, having the majority, having the machinery, having everything under his control, can provide ways and means to meet the reasonable, the just demands which my hon. friend has made on behalf of this great county of Victoria and Haliburton. There is no insuperable difficulty in the way, and nobody knows that better than the right hon. gentleman. If this constituency is not getting justice, surely it is not too late to remedy the defect. The Prime Minister can fix this matter with a stroke of his pen, he can ,do justice to this constituency, and I hope that, after the very clear and forcible statement, and the unanswerable argument presented by the hon. member for South Victoria (Mr. Vrooman), this schedule will be allowed to stand in the meantime, and that the right hon. gentleman will provide for the necessary additional representation which is so urgently demanded by the representative for South Victoria.

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext: I think the member for South Victoria wants a little more than sympathy from his hon friend from Toronto (Mr. Clarke). It is not improbable, when the member for Toronto finds the city in which he lives is gaining a representative, while many other sections of the country are losing, that he will move an amendment and have this additional member placed in the county of Victoria. So far as I am personally concerned, I would be pleased to support such a proposition. I sympathize with the hon. member for South Victoria and with his constituents in having to lose one member.

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS

speechtext:
I have already had the privilege of addressing this committee, or conference, that was appointed to determine the boundaries of the various ridings of Canada. As the Minister of Public Works very properly stated, I appeared
before the committee some months ago, when it proposed to add this provisional county of Haliburton to the district of Muskoka. I then showed to the committee the absolute impossibility, from a physical view point, of getting from one of these districts to the other, although they adjoined. There-is but one road connecting the two. I shall not here enter into all the arguments that, on four or five occasions, I presented to the committee, to show that Haliburton should not be added to Muskoka. They have no association whatever in common. The excellent item from the Toronto' ' News,' which the hon. member for South Victoria (Mr. Vrooman) has quoted, is in error in stating that Haliburton is not united with Victoria. Haliburton, under chapter 3 of the Revised Statutes of Ontario, is part of Victoria county. The same judge who presides over the citizens of the county of Victoria, presides over the citizens of the provisional county of Haliburton. The jurymen from every municipality in the provisional county of Haliburton attend the same courts in the town of Lindsay as do those in Victoria county ; so do the members of the bar in connection with the division courts. The same judge holds division courts all through Haliburton and Victoria. So far as it is possible for Haliburton to be added to any place for municipal and judicial purposes, it is added to the county of Victoria. I am free to say that I think the committee at the beginning w'ere in error in regard to the relationship which existed between Haliburton and Victoria. I verily believe that if the committee, in the early days, before their schedule was drawn up, and before they had formed the plan in their own minds which is now before the House, if we could have known that they were labouring under this misconception, .1 believe, from the spirit the committee showed in two or three cases, we could have induced them to give the provisional county of Haliburton and Victoria two members. I have faith in the right hon.' Prime Minister and I have faith in the hon. Minister of Public Works, the one representing the province of Ontario, and the other representing the Dominion. The hon. Minister of Justice was also very solicitous to see that fair play was done if we could point out a county from which we could take another member. But, it is a very difficult thing to ask a man to stand up in this House and say that Lanark shall be deprived of one member, or that Leeds, or Brockville, should be deprived of one member, or that Middlesex should be deprived of a member, although I would run the risk of saying that Middlesex should be deprived of a member and that West Northumberland should be done away with and that we should have one member for the county of Northumberland. But it puts a man in a delicate position to ask him to stand up and say that the constituency of some other member should be sacrificed

instead of his own. I realize that position. The other day I took the opportunity of pointing out the situation in Victoria and Haliburton on the map of the department drawn accurately to scale and which shows the area of these two counties. In this matter I am not going to mislead the House. I have never undertaken to mislead the House or the country, and I never shall.

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext:
I am glad the hon. gentlemen appreciate it. I hope that the right hon. Prime Minister and his colleagues will see their way clear to doing justice to Victoria and Haliburton by giving them two members. Victoria riding is a large one. It is folly to attempt, as has been done by hon. gentlemen opposite in this debate and in others, to deceive the people in reference to the geography and topography of the country. There are no settlers in a portion of this area and I do not think there will be very many. It is true that the county of Victoria is fairly well traversed by railways, but owing to the great area of the county and the fact that the right hon. Prime Minister has laid down the proposition that these large areas are entitled to a larger representation than the older settled localities together with the fact that the district is rising in importance, that there are numerous water-powers being developed and utilized, that there are cement works being established which will increase the population to a great extent and that people are going into the northern part of Victoria county and to the edge of Haliburton, an additional representative should be given to the district if it is at all possible. I know we cannot get it by force of arms. The hon. Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) pointed out the other day an occasion where I should turn out the militia and seek to carry something by force of arms. I trust the day is far distant when it will be necessary for us to resort' to arms. I appeal to the fair-play of hon. gentlemen opposite and ask their consideration on behalf of Victoria and Haliburton. I do not want to ask that Lanark, or Brockville, or Middlesex, or Northumberland, or Brant should give up one member. It places a man in an unenviable position to do so but I ask the right hon. Prime Minister in view of the facts that I have presented to the Committee on this occasion as well as on other occasions to accept the amendment which had been moved by the lion.' member for South Victoria to-night and which was moved by the hon. leader of the opposition in the committee long ago. Hon. gentlemen opposite will remember that it was moved in the committee, that it was impressed upon them then and having seen the justice of holding Haliburton and Victoria together as one county as they really are, I trust they will see their way clear, if at all possible, before this Bill is Mr. HUGHES (Victoria).
finally made law, to giving these counties two members.

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext:
I have listened with great interest and with every possible attention to the argument presented by my hon. friend from North Victoria (Mr. Hughes) but it seems to me that the preponderance of argument is altogether in favour of the proposition that Haliburton should be annexed to Victoria. The hon. gentleman stated that there were 23 townships in Haliburton. That is true, but in these twenty-three townships there are only
6,000	people. I asked my hon. friend to name the number of townships which were inhabited and be gave the names of nine and possibly ten, so that there are at least half of the townships which are not inhabited, and which are not likely to be inhabited. Therefore, we must take the position as it is. I notice the statement which has been made by my hon. friend that the population of Haliburton largely go through Victoria, that the way of communication leads through Victoria, that there is'a mountain in the riding which makes part of it uninhabitable. Under such circumstances it seems to me that all the natural conditions point to the fact that Haliburton should be added to Victoria. I look upon this point hs settled. Not only is it settled here but we find that while the minority in the committee proposed to give Victoria and Haliburton two members they annexed Haliburton to Victoria. Therefore I think we cannot do better than support the decision of the committee that Victoria and Haliburton should be allied together in one constituency. Whether they should have two members is a question, but, as my hon. friend has pointed out with very great force, and the argument has not been answered yet, you cannot give Victoria and Haliburton two members unless you take a member from some other constituency. No one has yet come forward to say:	I will sacrifice
myself on the altar of outraged virtue. I will give up my constituency. I am sure that the two ridings of Lanark do not care to give up one of their members, that Northumberland will not give up one of its members nor any other constituency. One of the things that we have to fight against in this redistribution is the determination of everybody to keep what he has. ' What we have we'll hold * is the doctrine that applies here. Those who have two members want still to have two, those who have three want three and those that have four want four. I am anxious to give two to Victoria and Haliburton and if I thought I could get a seconder at all I should attempt to gratify the wishes of my hon. friend and of the hon. member for South Victoria (Mr. Vrooman), but there does not seem to be any anxiety in any part of the province to give up any portion of the representation they have. This Bill, however, is creating a new consti-

tuency. The Bill is giving a constituency to the city of Toronto which it had not before. My hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) made a strong appeal to me. He stated that I could do almost anything in this House. I cannot ; that would be too much, but with his help, perhaps, 1 can do something and if my hon. friend will sec nd this proposition I will move :
That the following words be added to the amendment ' that section 54 of the schedule be stricken out and that the representation of the city of Toronto shall continue to be four as it is at present.'

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext: If my right hon. friend (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) will pass the amendment over I will give it my most serious attention ; but surely, after what has been so forcibly and frankly stated by my hon. friend from North Victoria (Mr. Hughes) there can be no argument as against the fair and reasonable proposition which he presents. Does the right hon. gentleman know that his four colleagues who surround him represent Ontario constituencies, the united population of which is less than 90,000, actually 89,096, with a unit of representation for these four counties of North and South Oxford, North York and Brant of 22,274 ; that these are old, well, settled, solid counties where the rural population is not increasing to any extent, but rather where the rural population is decreasing ; that this district of Haliburton and! Victoria has a larger area than probably the whole four counties, and that notwithstanding its great area and its population of 38.511

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext: What are the four counties ?

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext:
North Oxford, South Oxford, North York and Brant. I will give the hon. Minister of Public Works tHon. Mr. Sutherland) the population and if I am wrong he can correct me. These are the populations of the constituencies represented by the Minister of the Crown, and here is my hon. friend (Mr. Vrooman) appealing that Victoria and Haliburton with a population
16,000	larger than the average population of these four constituencies, should have two members. Victoria and Haliburton has a population of 38,511, against an iverage population of 22,274 in the others. This county is one of the sparsely settled districts in Ontario, and it directly comes xnder the principle laid down by the right hon. gentleman the other day. But hon. gentlemen opposite have to-night laid down the new principle : ' What we have we'll hold.'i That is enunciated now as the guiding principle of the majority of the redistribution committee. The right hon. gentleman is anxious that the city of Toronto which has been so scandalously treated by this redistribution committee, should be deprived of the additional member which it is proposed to give it. Would there be any justice in that ? Since 1891, 64,000 people have been added to that city, and the unit of representation for the whole province is 25,383, but only one additional member is given Toronto for an increased population of 64,000. Would the right hon. gentleman seriously propose that the unit of representation for Toronto should be 52,000 and for the rest of file province of Ontario only
25,000	? The right hon. gentleman says that nobody seems disposed to give up his sfeat in order that an additional member may be given to Victoria and Haliburton. The responsibility for redistributing the representation of Ontario rests with the government, and the hon. member (Mr. Vroomain) has made out a strong case. The right hon. gentleman ought to assume the responsibility of providing an additional member for these united counties, even if he is obliged to take a member from some other county. If Toronto was given the representation it is entitled to, we would have seven or eight members instead of live, and surely the Prime Minister Is not serious in asking that the fifth member should be taken away, seeing that the unit of representation in Toronto under the proposed Bill is 42,000, while the unit for the rest of the province is 25,000. I trust that the Prime Minister will accede to the reasonable request made by the member for South Victoria.

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext:
I have often stated that it is impossible to give an urban population the same representation as a rural population. Montreal would be entitled to more representation than Toronto, if we were to apply to it the principle laid down by my bon. friend (Mr. Clarke). If we did apply that principle to Montreal, instead of having six members it would have at least perhaps twelve members. If we did that in Montreal we would have to wipe out of existence several constituencies in Quebec which would have the same objection to being decapitated as have the rural constituencies in Ontario. We could have done much more in the case of Montreal. Without interfering at all with the rural constituencies, we could have taken the surplus population of Montreal and added it to the adjacent rural constituencies, so that at least two of the members who sit in this House; my bon. "friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) and my hon. friend from Laval (Mr. Leonard); would have to fight for their lives, if they would not have been wiped out of existence altogether. We did not do that, we would not take advantage of our position. In the case of Victoria and Haliburton, if we gave it another member, we would have to take him from somewhere else, and if my hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) will take the responsibility of saying that we should take that member from one par-tieular place or another, we may consider the matter. I do not say that we would

agree to that, because rather than deprive a constituency of a member, I would prefer not to give life to a constituency which does not exist already. It seems to me that it is fairer to have it this way than any other way, and I think that ought to appeal to the sense of justice of my hon. friend.

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext:
The Prime Minister has stated that he would be glad to give an extra member to Victoria and Haliburton if he had it in his power to give Ontario eighty-seven members instead of eighty-six. I admit that the government has an onerous duty to perform, but the government must take the responsibility of performing that duty justly. Justice is no respecter of persons or constituencies, and in dividiug up the province of Ontario it naturally appeals to one's sense of justice that where you map out a district electing two members, there ought to be a larger population in that district than in a constituency which only elects one member. Had the government followed that rule, my hon. friend from Victoria (Mr. Vroomanj would not make his appeal in vain. The First Minister has said that the argument of the gentleman from North Victoria was convincing, that Haliburton must be attached to Victoria, I am not prepared to dispute that, nor do I think it necessary for my purpose to do so, but if that be the case, it simply points to the fact that having enlarged this district it is an additional reason why it should be represented by two members. Surely it is only fair to continue two members to the enlarged district. The First Minister asks us, who will give up his seat, but that is not the question. It is the duty of the government in redistributing the seats all over the province, not to give representation to constituencies whose population does not entitle them to representation. The aggregate population of the two North-umberlands is 33,500, and they have two members, whereas Victoria and Haliburton with a population of 38,511 is only to have one member. Following out the principle laid down by the First Minister, don't you think that the sparsely settled district of Victoria and Haliburton with a larger population, is much better entitled to two members than the older and more thickly populated district of Northumberland with a smaller population. If the argument of the Prime Minister is logical, it points to the fairness of giving Victoria and Haliburton two members while Northumberland and Durham is entitled to only one, because its population is only 33,550. and it is an old Settled' district. Take the two Lanarks, they have a less population than Victoria and Haliburton that is only given one member. North Lanark has a population of about 17,000, and South Lanark about 19,000, or an aggregate population of 37,233, and there they have two members representing Sir WILFRID LAURI3R.
fewer people than one member represents in Victoria and Haliburton.
Yet that is an old and thickly settled section of country. If the hon. genleman's logic amounts to anything, it clearly shows that his duty lies in the direction of giving two members to Victoria and Haliburton instead of two to Lanark. Justice is no respecter of persons or of constituencies, and justice demands that the government shall assume the responsibility of doing that duty. Take the three Middlesexes, in which the aggregate population represented by three men is 54,726-Bast Middlesex, 20,000; North Middlesex, 15,000, and West Middlesex, 18,000. Thus you find that three members represent very little more population than the one. Is that fair ? These constituencies belong to an old and thickly settled district ; and, by the hon. Prime Minister's contention, the new and sparsely settled- districts require a larger representation according to population than the old and thickly settled districts. If that be the case, why not give Middlesex one less, and give Victoria and Haliburton one more ? Would that not be. doing what is proper ? It may be that it would not be popular, but governments who take the responsibilities of office must sometimes do things that are unpopular. It is the duty of the government to take one member away from some of these counties which are represented by two members though having less population than Victoria or Haliburton, and give one member to that sparsely settled district, because it contains a very large area and a very small population.

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext: Lest there might he any possibility of misunderstanding my argument, I wish to point out that this is not the first, the second, the third, the fourth nor the fifth time this, session that I have fought this thing out. '

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext: You did not win as easily as usual.

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext: Yes, I won, and that is the reason I am following it up. The first proposition was to unite Haliburton and Muskoka. I appeared before the committee on two or three occasions and laid the facts fairly and squarely before it, and I won. They saw the righteousness of my position, and recognized it by placing Victoria and Haliburton together. I have more faith than some of my friends on this side of the House in the Prime Minister's fair-play.

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext: Carried.

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext:
They say flattery is a falsehood pleasantly told, and that blarney is tlie truth pleasantly told. I admit that I am addicted to blarney sometimes. As I say, I have fought this thing out. The members of the House have heard from * me on this issue before. First, I pointed

out the necessity of preserving the union that has existed between Victoria and Hali-burton for many years. 1 pointed out that they were two old counties, and that while hon. gentlemen opposite are making them one, they constitute two ridings for the legislative assembly of Ontario. I pointed out that the population in these counties is growing. I pointed out that a number of men who were in the habit of going to the lumber woods, and who were not counted in the census, have returned and taken up farms, apd have given up lumbering since it has gone above the height of land, and up to Lake Superior. I pointed out in the committee, and also in the House the other day that by the revised statutes of Ontario, chapter 3, which is taken as the basis of this measure, these counties are one and indivisible. 1 pointed out that the people of Haliburton come to the county of Victoria to trade. I pointed out that the Midland division of the Grand Trunk Railways ends at Haliburton, and that the Irondale, Bancroft and Ottawa Railway runs across the southern part of the riding, bringing people to Tory Hill, which I hope the Prime Minister will visit some day ; and Essonville, Gooderham, and Deer Lake are all on that line of the railway. . There are no lakes in Scotland or Ireland, not even the Lakes of Killarney, which can surpass in grandeur and beauty, the claim of the lakes in the counties of Haliburton and Victoria. There are only three wagon roads running into the county of Haliburton that do not come from the county of Victoria ; one is from Peterborough, one from Hastings, and one from Muskoka. The one from Muskoka is so impassable that it is rarely travelled. I think all parties in the county of Elgin are agreed on that point, in the next place, having laid down the principle, they think it is necessary in carrying it out, that no partiality should be shown to any county in the Dominion. Now whoa the light hon. gentleman introduced this measure, on the 31st of March, he proposed what he thought should be the unit of representation for the Dominion of Canada, which was a little over 25,000. But since then a unit has been agreed upon by the committee appointed to make this redistribution, by which there should be one member for at least 24,381 people ; for every two members there should be at least 36,572 ; for every three members there should be 60,953 people. Those units the people of Elgin, Conservatives and Liberals, are prepared to accept and to carry out in the spirit with which the Prime Minister introduced this Bill. When the committee
undertook to redistribute the county of Elgin, they found certain municipalities in it that did not rightly belong to the county. The committee found the town of Ridgetown and the townships of Orford and Howard in West Elgin, and they concluded to take these three municipalities out of West Elgin and place them elsewhere. I want to say that so far as that is concerned there is no difference of opinion on this side of the House with our hon. friends opposite. On the other hand, they observed in the eastern riding of Elgin that the village of Springfield and the municipality of South Dorchester were located in Middlesex county, and they concluded, in order to make the eastern riding of Elgin right, to take Springfield and South Dorchester from Middlesex and place them in Elgin county, where they rightly belong. Now I want to say that up to this point there is no difference of opinion, no fault is found. I fully approve of the action of the committee so far, because I expect that municipal boundary lines shall be observed so far as possible, and they are being observed up to this point.
