Robinson, who was elected and sits on this side of the House. No correct estimate could be formed, therefore, of the Liberal majority in West Elgin in 1900, and so the hon. member for Bothwell took the majority for Mr. Casey in 1896, and gave credit to the government for having a majority of 726 in West Elgin. There is nothing unfair about that. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Clan-cy) showed that in 1896, Mi-. Charlton had a majority in North Norfolk over the Conservative candidate of 544, making a total majority of 1,270 for the Liberals in these two constituencies. There was no contest in North Norfolk in 1900, and consequently the hon. gentleman had to refer to the election of 1896. In 1896 you had a Conservative representing Nipisslng, and he was elected by a majority of 90l! It is true that a Liberal was returned from that constituency at the last election. I was surprised to hear the right hon. the Prime Minister refer to Nipissing. Every man who has paid any attention to politics knows that there are certain constituencies in this country which, as a rule, go with the government in power in a by-election. Now, what occurred in Nipissing ? The



election was to have been held in that constituency on general election day as in all other constituencies, but there was a little manipulation, arid the returning officer was stowed away in a little room on nomination day so that he might prevent the election in Nipissing being held on the day of the general elections. And why was that ? It was known that if the election was held after the general elections that the party in power would have the advantage, and so the election was postponed. In view of these circumstances, the election in 1900 was no fair test of the relative strength of the two parties in Nipissing. Then we come to North Waterloo, and North Waterloo, as every one knows, elected a Conservative bv acclamation in 1900, so that the only rule we could go by was the majority given for the Conservative candidate in 1890. which was 309. Therefore, we have 1,270 on the Liberal side of the account and 1,273 on the Conservative side of the account, or a difference of three in favour of the Conservative party. What was the object of the Prime Minister claiming a large majority in Nipissing in the last election ? It was not a fair thing for the Prime Minister to do. in view of the manipulation which I have shown of that election. The only fair thing to do was to take the majority given in 189ti. as was done by my hon.'friend from Both well. I simply point out these things to show that the Prime Minister is very much biased in his judgment in reference to this redistribution, and it is because of that bias that he has fallen into the trap of defending this redistribution. which has been made largely for the purpose of political gain to the Liberal party. I am sorry to have to say that, and having expressed my views in as brief a manner as possible with respect to this matter. I can only come to the conclusion that this is a redistribution solely in the interest of the Liberal party in this country.

That in the opinion of this House it is necessary for the welfare of Canada that the annual expenditure relative 'to legislation should be kept within reasonable bounds. Therefore, this House asks the Dominion government of Canada to petition the British government to so amend the British North America Act that the matter of representation to the Dominion parliament and the provincial legislatures may be reduced in accordance with the wishes of the Canadian people. That this House believes that the work of legislation would be more economically, expeditiously and efficiently done, if the members of this House were reduced one-half of its number. And that the Senate, if not entirely abolished, should be reduced to one-half of its number, and elected by the people. liament; and whenever it is possible county-boundaries shall be respected.
I placed that resolution on the Order Paper three years ago, and I have not changed my mind in regard to it. But I do not want to commence with the county of Elgin. I want the county of Elgin served the same as all other counties, and I am satisfied that the people of Elgin, who are intelligent and broad-minded people, are willing to send one member if that is made the rule. I can assure you that they will elect the best man they have, and you may be sure that he is not far off. I am not afraid to trust my case in the hands of the people of the county of Elgin, because they know that I am here working in their interest. Now, I do not expect this resolution to be carried in this House, but I hope that this government will have courage enough, as they have the power, with a majority of forty-five at their back, to consider this matter at their next caucus, and petition the Imperial government to give them this power. See liow such a reduction in the number of members would result in economy ; see how much more quickly we would get through with our work. We would have got away two months ago if we had a membership of only 100 in this House. Our laws are not like the laws of the Medes and Persians ; we can change them when we think proper to do so in the interest of the people. This government, with all the ability they boast of, ought to try to economize, and they can do it in no better way than by reducing the number of members in this House, in the Senate and in the local legislatures. A man said to me the other day, more power to your elbow ; and if we had more independent men in the House, we would have a better government and a different Canada.

speechtext: It is unfortunate that the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Thomson) diid not submit some facts to this committee, to attempt to at least justify the wild statements he has made. He has used most extreme language, talking of scandalous gerrymanders and vicious acts on the part of the government, of things that the majority ought to be ashamed of, and so on; yet he has not produced the slightest evidence of anything of that kind. He would set himself up ns a paragon of virtue, as one far better than other lion, gentlemen in this House, as one who would not support anything that was not fair and right between the two parties. He objects to a difference of between two and three thousand in the population of two constituencies. Yet, this very day lie voted for an amendment that made a difference of between four and five thousand between two constituencies, simply because the displacing of one large township would make a hive in the interest of his party, and for no other reason. My hon. friend (Mr. Thomson, Grey) must know that there is no occasion for such wild language as he has used. Some time ago, when language of this kind was used. I prophesied that when we came to discuss the arrangement of constituencies on their merits, hon. gentlemen opposite would hardly find one that would justify reasonable criticism, to say nothing of the wild accusations such as the hon. gentleman has made. We are willing to compare the propositions we have made with those submitted by hon. gentlemen. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Thomson, (Grey) has an amendment which, if carried, would make two ridings with a difference in population of about 10,000. Without any regard to political associations or community of interest, business or otherwise, he proposes in his amendment to violate every principle, every rule and every regard to common decency, and then he gets up and makes wild and reckless statements about the action of this committee. I say he has no reason for saying that. I am willing to admit that the limits of these ridings had to be changed. They were made up of townships from other ridings previously, and in going back to county boundaries the limits had to be changed.

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext: Was any portion of any other county in Grey before ?

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext: My hon. friend just mentioned Dufferin.

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext: Dufferin was never recognized in the electoral division of Hastings before this Bill.

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext:
We are dealing with municipal counties yet, it is a municipal county yet under the Ontario Act, and the hon. gentleman says it .was pever a municipal county under Dominion legislation. Dominion legislation has nothing to do with creating a municipal county. I say that county had to be dealt with, and any fair-minded man would make the division geographically, and it appears to me that the present limits of the north ridings are better than those he proposes. The territory is more compact, the community of interest is greater, if we were

*well informed in the committee. Then as to the others, it is a question of whether you place the two townships in one constituency or the other. On that point the non. gentleman might appeal to the good sense of the House instead of getting up and making these wild and extravagant statements for which he has not a tittle of evidence. That is not the way to appeal to any Committee if he wishes to secure a change. We discussed this in the committee with the members for the county and other people, and surely the people having a right to ne heard in this matter as well as the member for North Grey. While this proposition did not meet the views of all the people in the district, 1 believe it has met with the approval and is in accordance with the wishes of the great majority of the people of the county.

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext: I do not intend to take any lecture from the Minister of Public Works in a matter that affects my constituency. I look upon him as one of the chief perpetrators of this gerrymander, indeed I look upon him as the responsible head of that committee, the one who has helped to vote down the resolutions which were put forward to divide these constitu-tncies fairly. Yet the Minister of Public Works stands up and tells me that, taking the townships out of the south riding of Grey and placing them in a constituency which already has a much larger population, is dividing this riduig fairly, making it compact and equalizing the population. Why, the division on the face of it is a gerrymander, and I repeat again that it is scandalous gerrymander of which the committee ought to be ashamed.

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext: The people of Grey will judge of that.

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext: I think the remarks of the Minister of Public Works call for some answer. I understood him to say that there was no person asking for the changes which i.re proposed to-night. Well, he must certainly forgot that the members for Grey appeared before the committee and presented strong arguments in favour of the redistribution in the manner contained in the amendment offered by the ho:i. Member for South Grey (Mr. Richardson).

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext: The bon. gentleman misunderstood me, I did not make any such statement. I did say that the members appeared before the committee.

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext:
Perhaps I misunderstood him. But I wish to say that it does seem strange to me that, notwithstanding that three of us went before that committee and presented onr reasons in favour of the plan of redistribution which we offered to the committee, after we bad done that, it was Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND.
simply voted down without a word of argument being advanced against it, without ,any reasons being offered why our plan should not be accepted. There was no effort to convince us that the proposal of the government was better than ours, but our plan was simply suppressed. Now, in going before that committee we relied upon the fairness of the Prime Minister, and I could not help but believe that at least we might expect justice, that we might expect that the ridings would remain very much as they were, while recognizing that it was necessary to rearrange the limits so as to make the population as nearly equal as possible.
I bad that impression because the Prime Minister bad put himself on record in 1S92, with regard to the last redistribution, in these words :
What I propose to the sense of justice of every man in this House is that this application of the law shall be made in .such a manner as that both parties shall remain with the same advantages they now possess.
Now, that is all we ask-rearrange the population so as to equalize it, and allow the people to remain with the same advantages which they have had heretofore. There was another pronouncement made on this question which I will read for the benefit of tbe Minister of Public Works anc of the Prime Minister himself. Speaking at that time the Prime Minister said :
The proposition I lay down is that under the Bill one party should not gain an advantage over the other.
Now, I want to ask if that is the case in the redistribution of Grey. Does not one party gain an advantage over tbe other? Let me analyse it for a minute. For many years North Grey was represented by a Reformer, but the present representative of North Grey (Mr. Thomson) carried it by a majority. Tbe minister bad a majority of 163. According to the proposed Bill that majority is taken away from him and added to East Grey where the Conservative majority was already large. Now, was not that giving an unfair advantage to one party? They . stuck on to him the townships of St. Vincent and Meaford, which give a Liberal majority of 76, they took off the township of Holland which gives a Conservative majority of 130, and they took off the township of Sullivan which gave a Conservative majority of 76; in other words they took away 273 of his Conservative support. Was that carrying out the principle laid down by the Prime Minister ? Has the Prime Minister carried out the principle that he solemnly laid down in 1892 ? In my judgment he has done the reverse. Now, I naturally asked what was the motive of the hon. gentleman in making these changes. I can see no other motive except a political one. Because in making these changes you I have not put the municipalities together

where a community of interest called for it, the compactness of the riding is no more uniform, the equalization of the population is not better in any respect than under the plan proposed by the members who now represent the county of Grey. Therefore, if there is no other thing accomplished the one thing that is accomplished is that it weakens the two ridings that send Conservatives to this House, takes away the entire majority and many more votes that they had in their election and makes these two ridings eminently Liberal. That is accomplished if nothing else is. We have a right to assume that the only motive was a political one. When we take South Grey what do we find there ? South Grey gave the present sitting member a majority of 142. They took away Artemesia which gave him 250 of a majority and they took away Mark-dale which gave him 80 of a majority, or 330 in all. The member for South Grey had a majority of 142 so that evidently the constituency is left hopelessly Reform.

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext: Hopelessly ?

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext: Hopelessly, I say, as far as the Conservative party is concerned. They have taken away all the majority which both of these members had and many more besides. Therefore it is evident that they must have had one object in view and that is .a political one. How does that agree with the statement made by the right hon. leader of the government in 1892 when he laid down the principle that this redistribution should be carried out in such a way that it would not give one political party any advantage over the other, and when he also laid down the principle that you shall allow the constituencies to remain as far as possible where they were before, unless it is absolutely necessary to change them on account of the change of population in the locality. Take the county of Grey. The changes wre proposed would make the population in North Grey 23,407, in East Grey 24,290, and in South Grey 21,812. That is nearer the unit of representation than would be attained under the proposition made by the government. Was there any other motive ? Some one jocularly said that the government proposed this arrangement of the county of Grey out of respect for the Grand Master of the Orange Association. I would like to be charitable enough to believe that that was so, but, after reading the speech made by the right hon. gentleman at Chicoutimi in which he thanked God there were no Orangemen in his party, I can only come to the conclusion that it was done to make a Conservative hive and that he was desirous of keeping the Orangemen away as far as possible while giving the Grand Master an opportunity of being returned to this House.

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext: That was before he knew you well.

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext: I have sat in this House with the right hon. gentleman for a very much longer time than the hon. member for Guys-borough (Mr. Fraser has, so that he knows me very well. I have given these reasons to show that East Grey would have been fairer in population, better in community of interest and more compact in form if the redistribution had been carried out on the lines we proposed. I have a map here showing Grey as it is to-day. There is East Grey, there is North Grey and there is South Grey.

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext: What is that white patch in the centre ?

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext: That is South Grey which goes from there across there and runs up there. As it was before, East Grey weut right up that line to the lake and Artemesia was taken out of the centre of it. As we propose it the line would run straight through the country from the south to the north. That would make the population all right, it would make community of interest all right because the people in the north deal in Thornbury and Meaford and Collingwood, the people in the north-east in Collingwood and the people in the south and west in Markdale. So that, the community of interest, the conformation of the riding and the equality of population, or the unit of representation, would be better under the proposal which we make than under the one which the government have made. Now then, St. Vincent and Meaford are taken out of East Grey and added to North Grey and the only reason why that is done is that St. Vincent and Meaford give a Reform majority of 76 and they take away the majority that was received by my hon. friend from North Grey (Mr. Thomson) so that they may help in future to elect a Reformer. But they take away Holland as well which gave my hon. friend 130 of a majority and they add that to East Grey. Therefore in no sense can it be regarded as a better arrangement than the one which we propose or quite as good. In view of that I am disposed to support the amendment made by my hon. friend from South Grey because I believe it is a fail-one. It is fair in regard to population, in regard to community of interest, in regard to the commercial interests of the people and in. regard to the conformation of the riding, and it proposes to maintain that which has been for many years the condition of things in that county with the exception of taking Artemesia out which we naturally expect will be taken out because the township of Melanchton which has a population of about 4,000 is taken out of East Grey and put in Dufferin.

We all know that the measure which was before this House at that time was a measure providing for the redistribution of the constituencies. But I think it would be unfair to attempt to satisfy the opposition in the House because nothing can satisfy them.
I would like to know whether that hon. gentleman is of the same opinion to-day.

Their conduct is a pretext to waste the time of this House from day to day and from week to week.

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext: Is the hou. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) still of opinion, that in a matter of this kind the government should not go even half way to meet the opposition ?

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext:
That depends entirely upon the proposals made by the opposition. If the opposition submit reasonable proposals, on the line of the declared principle of the government, then the government should meet them half way ; but, if the opposition submits unreasonable propositions that no government could fairly accept, then I say :

don't meet them half way. Now, Sir, I confess that I would rather have left in my riding the townships which have been taken from it. although they always have given a majority against me. The people of those townships are most respectable and reasonable people, and I would not have the slightest objection to trust my chances in their hands. I have no reason to complain because my majority has not been strengthened ; it has been strengthened beyond all reason, but I do complain that the principle laid down by the Prime Minister has been violated. He said :
The proposition I lay down is that under the Bill one party should not gain an advantage over the other.
Here you have taken away the Conservative majority in North Grey, and the Conservative majority in South Grey, and you have them added to the Conservative majority in East Grey, which was already very large. I have no reason to complain of that, personally, but I do complain that it violates the principle laid down by the First Minister in 1882, when he said that one party should not gain an advantage over another in a redistribution Bill.

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext: It is agreed by all that the present representation of Grey has to be amended. My hon. friends from South Grey, and from East Grey, and from North Grey, agree that the present shape of the riding should be remodelled, and the only difference is as to how that should be done. The question at issue is, whether the division should be made up and down, or crosswise. Now. take the map presented by the hon. member for North Grey to-night, and take the map of the ridings as we propose, and look at this picture and on that. This proposition of the committee makes a compact riding.

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext: Bet me point out where that division is not suitable. There are two towns in the county where the people do their business, one being Meaford, in the east, and the other Owen Sound in the west, so that these divisions are separated commercially.

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext: There may be something in that. I am not familiar with the local conditions and I cannot know whether the people do their business in one part of the riding or in another, but I look upon the shape of the riding as it is.

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext: Would the Prime Minister allow me to say that the people living in this part of the riding sent a joint petition irrespective of politics to the leader of the opposition and to the Prime Minister, asking to be joined in that constituency.

speechtext:
At all events, there is compactness and equalization in the proposition submitted by the committee, and
that is what I contended for in 1892. By the redistribution which we propose, East Grey will have a population of 23.663; North Grey, 24.874. and South Grey, 21,053-SO. so that there is little discrepancy of population. and there is a marked improvement in that respect over the existing ridings. But there is something very insidious in this map which the hon. gentleman has displayed. This little red corner represents the village of Markdale, which I understand is the residence of the hon. gentleman for East Grey, and which we want to place in the riding which he represents. I daresay there would lie some comment on our illiber-ality if we were to put that village into South Grey.

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext: It is misrepresented on that map.

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext: Yes, it is misrepresented on the map. The village is partly in three different townships-Glen-elg, Artemesia and Holland-is it not?

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext: No, in two.

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext: In two only ; but in this map it is put into one. If it is partly in East Grey and partly in South Grey, is it not fairer that it should be put altogether in East Grey, being the place of residence of the member who represents' East Grey ? If we did not do so, I think my hon. friend from East Grey would be the first to find fault. He does not find fault, but the hon. member for North Grey does. Whatever we do, hon. gentlemen opposite find fault.

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext: I may tell the right hon. gentleman that although 1 have represented East Grey for the last twenty-five years, for the last twenty years, I have not lived in it, but have lived in Markdale.

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext: We are making the representation to accord with the facts, and making it possible for my hon. friend to reside in his own riding. I cannot understand the sinister motives which the hon. gentleman attributes to me. It is true, I do not agree with my hon. friend in religion, in polities, and perhaps in many other things, but if he is to continue to be the member for East Grey, my heart will not be broken if he has a larger majority than before.

maintopic: BEVT8ED EDITION- COMMONS
speechtext: When the Prime Minister was giving some apparent reason, a very weak one, why the village of Mark-dale should be put into East Grey, as affecting my hon. friend from East Grey, he did not say anything as to how it would affect the member for South Grey. I may state that the larger portion of the village of Markdale is situated in the township of Glenelg. It is true, it is on the boundarv line, and part of it is in the township of Artemesia, but the larger portion of it is

speechtext: in Glenelg, which lies geographically in South Grey.

speechtext: The map which was submitted to the committee showed that this village was partly in three townships, and that two of the townships were in East Grey and one in South Grey.

maintopic: COMMOXS
speechtext: Two-thirds of that village are in Glenelg, which is in South Grey. South Grey had the smallest population of the three ridings, being some 2,500 less than that of East Grey, and yet the committee took this village from South Grey and put it in East Grey, making the disparity greater still. Although I have asked the Minister of Public Works for some satisfactory reason why this was done, I have failed to get any reply. I think it might vet be in order for the Minister of Public Works to reply to my question, if there was any attempt made by the committee to carry out those principles which were laid down for its guidance, and which it was supposed would be exercised in the subdivision of this county as in the case of others.

maintopic: COMMOXS
speechtext: I have no doubt that the statement made by the Premier did affect this matter, and that it was considered that the village was the residence of my hon. friend who represents East Grey. Outside of that, we are not children. We all know that townships have a certain population, that the people in them are divided in politics, and that when you come to delimit the ridings in a county, one party will be affected more or less. But I do maintain that we have divided them to the best of our knowledge and ability. We have not undertaken to give the Conservative party all their own way, so that they e-mld destroy all the chances of their political opponents ; but they have not been able to show that any improper or undue advantage has been taken of them in any riding. I say again, I am prepared to compare propositions. There must be more or less politics in these matters.

maintopic: COMMOXS
speechtext: More or less.

maintopic: COMMOXS
speechtext: I am perfectly sincere in this matter. I do not want to go back and speak of how hon. gentlemen opposite treated the late member for South Grey in days gone by, cheating him out of his seat. We are resting our action in these cases on the judgment of the people of this county, who are just as capable of knowing whether this is a fair division as the hon. member for West Toronto is-perhaps more, because they have taken some interest in it, and are more fair in their judgment. What I say is that you cannot place a municipality in one riding or in another without more or less changing the political complexion of the riding ;

maintopic: COMMOXS
speechtext: but I do say that there has not been yet, and will not be, in the discussion of this measure, anything to show that the members of the committee were grossly unfair or took any party advantage more than they were perfectly entitled to take in the divisions they were making. They have been fair to their opponents, and if any fault is to be found with them, it is rather by their political friends than by members of the opposition.

maintopic: COMMOXS
speechtext: If the hon. minister would properly inform himself, he would know that it was a Conservative who represented South Grey from 1878 to 1882, when the change was made in the representation, and that from that time up to the last parliament, it was represented by a Reformer. So that no Reformer was cheated out of his seat

At that time the right hon. gentleman promised us a fair measure of redistribution. and following him in that debate I accepted bis statement in the spirit in which it was made. But having laid the matter before the committee, and not having obtained what I considered justice to the county, I intend to appeal to the right hon. gentleman himself and ask him to look Into the geographical division of the county, and see whether the division made by the committee is really wihat can be called a fair and equitable one. I do not know how far the right hon. gentleman has knowledge of the townships of the county of Hastings and their conditions, but I may inform him that in that county there are twenty-four townships. The county is three townships wide and eight deep. It is about 125 to 130 miles from the south end to the north end, and. roughly speaking, 33 miles wide. Under the former division, Hastings had three members. And, while I think I could well argue on the floor of this House that Hastings is still entitled to three members, and while I believe that, if the right hon. gentleman would go into the matter and compare Hastings with other constituencies he would see that we are entitled to three members, I am not pressing that. I am not admitting that we are not entitled to three members, on the contrary, I am claiming that we are entitled to that number. But, as I desire to avoid the possibility of an answer to what I am saying, I am merely

asking the Prime Minister to view the fact that we are entitled to three members and have been only given two, as if possible, an additional reason why he should be particularly astute to see that, in such a case, the promise he has made is fairly and faithfully carried out. When we look at the twenty-four townships it would strike the ordinary person that if any endeavour is made to make a fair division, there should be twelve townships, if possible in each riding. According to the scheme now before us, the county is divided into East and West Hastings, with seven townships in West Hastings, seventeen townships in East Hastings. If we look at the geographical area of the two, it must be admitted that that area is not fairly divided. If the right lion, gentleman will look at the population, he will find that the population of West Hastings which has only seven townships, is 32,504, while the population of East Hastings, with seventeen townships, is 26,786. One would naturally ask, why is it that the population of the West Riding is about 6,000 more than the population of the East Riding 7 If the right lion, gentleman will look at the returns of the last general election for that county, he will see that it would he impossible to give to East Hastiugs any single township adjoining it without improving the political chances of the opposition in their riding. As a matter of fact the committee has massed nine municipalities-seven townships and two other divisions, one city and one town-every one of which will give a Conservative majority, while the remainder of seventeen townships and two other municipalities have been set apart as East Hastings, in the hope that the government, may, peradventure, acquire a supporter from that part of the county. When the matter was before the committee, the only reaon given by the majority for this extraordinary division was that the rule had been laid down that, where there was an urban population and also a rural population in a same constituency to winch two members were given, the division that had the urban part should have a larger population than that which had the rural part. Now, I am not going to quarrel with that division; but I would point out that, in order to secure the difference of about 6,000 for West Hastings over East Hastings, what might be called a bay window lias been thrown out into what should naturally be and would properly be the riding of East Hastings. If the right bon. gentleman lias the map before him, he can follow what I say, and, If not, I will he happy to furnish him with one. He will see, at the bottom of the riding the city of Belleville, now in West Hastings, which lies in the township of Thuriow, which is one of the townships of East Hastings. It is true that Belleville was in the riding of West Hastings when the divisions were different from what is now contemplated. But the old three ridings Mr. NORTHRUP.
have been abolished and the committee have undertaken to form two ridings out of the three. They took the three townships, first Sydney to the west, Thuriow and Thyen-dinaga, and the city of Belleville which was wholly located in Thuriow which is one of the townships'Of East Hastings. Belleville gives a Conservative majority so it has to he left in West Hastings, where it was before. So, on the south we have a bay window for the city of Belleville. Then running twelve or fourteen miles north we have another bay window to take in the townships of Huntington and Rawdon. I venture to say that no reason can be suggested for Raw'don and Huntington being added to West Hastings, except that they give Conservative majorities, and they are to be added to a riding which will have a Conservative majority of 1,200.

should go into East Hastings. As a matter of fact, as long ago as the redistribution of 1S92 Huntington should have been put into East Hastings, because it would have made the riding four townships instead of three, as it is now, and would have equalized the population by bringing East Hastings up to about 20,000, with North Hastings about 22,000. It was not done at that time, because nothing was done in that part of the country, and Sir John Thompson declined to make an exception of any one place. But, if the committee desires to divide the county fairly and would look at the present North Hastings as to be divided between fiast and West Hastings, the first thing to strike him would be that Huntington should be added to East Hastings and thereby make a square, four townships and add a couple of thousand to population. If we take the present West Hastings and run a line to the north we can get all the population required-and that is the only reason given to the committee for the proposed scheme-and we could have two compact ridings instead of having two distorted ridings as proposed. If the Minister of Public Works would take the figures of population he will see that, starting with 9.000 in Belleville and 4,217 in Trenton, if he takes one tier of townships from the south to the north and a couple of tiers across, he can have twelve townships in West Hastings and leave twelve townships for East Hastings, he can have a population of whatever amount he requires. If he wishes the urban population to exceed that of the rural constituency he can have it by merely adding more townships on the north. Then that will leave East Hastings a compact riding two townships broad from north to south, whatever the length might be.
I think it is fair to call attention to this fact, that when the census was taken a short time ago, as will appear from the papers brought down before the Public Accounts Committee, one of the commissioners in North Hastings was paid an extraordinarily large sum, $600 or $700, on the strength of the letters which he wrote giving explanations of the difficult country which he had to traverse. If the Minister of Public Works will investigate the subject and read the letters which are on file in the department, he will understand the difficulties which were admitted by the government since they paid him this very large sum-
I am not saying it was excessive-but it was a sum of some $600 including a bonus of $300, becausa, as he pointed out, the roads were the worst roads in the Dominion of Canada, the population was sparse, and it was almost impossible to journey about. Therefore the government admitted his statements and increased his commission for these reasons. Now, if that be the case, surely I can appeal to the Premier and say that if an appeal is to be made to the country, it is a practical impossibility for either
side, it is impossible for whoever may be supporting the right lion, gentleman or whoever may be supporting the leader of the opposition, to canvass a riding which is 128 miles long and about 150 miles from the south-east to the north-west, and as the sheriff of our county said a few days ago, if stretched on the map, the riding of east Hastings would stretch almost from Belleville to Hamilton. I think therefore I may Say that twelve townships are as many as any man can canvass in the next general election in view of the almost impassable roads in that region. To endeavour to cover seventeen townships under the circumstances I have detailed is to ask an impossibility from any man.
Then there is another point to be considered. The only railway we have running to the north at the present time, the Central Ontario Railway, skirts along the west riding of Hastings, and the majority of the people of East Hastings going from south to north have to journey over to the west and take the railway running north through West Hastings, and then they are left at the west side of the riding. The tier of townships of which West Hastings is composed is as far as they can go by railway. Then we are compelled to drive over this enormous extent of country with practically impassable roads. There is another consideration. Suppose both political parties desired to have some place where they could hold a convention and discuss political affairs. No hon. gentleman opposite can suggest a place in the riding of East Hastings as proposed to be constituted, in which a political meeting or convention of either side could be held with any practical success. Tweed is about the only place suggested. Tweed is in the present riding of East Hastings. If we are to have our meeting in Tweed the men from the north would have to go through six townships, about 100 miles. They would have to go due south from the northern part of the riding through a region in which there is no railway and with impassable roads to reach Tweed. I do not speak of my personal knowledge, but I have been told by an authority on which I rely that as a matter of fact you cannot drive from the north end of this riding to the south because it is a physical impossibility, there are no roads over which any man can drive from the north side of this riding to the south. You must go over into West Hastings and drive down West Hastings and then drive over to East Hastings. I presume the committee must have had some principle in view at the time they made this arrangement, as I take it for granted the right hon. Premier has no desire to withdraw from the position he took and that he is willing to give a fail-division of the riding. I think I can ask the committee to give some reason that would justify any such division as this. The ridings are called East and West Hastings.

Mr. Chairman, having the honour to represent one of the ridings of Hastings, I feel that I have a right to discuss this question and that it would be expected that I would discuss it, but at the same time I would like it to be understood that I do not discuss this question of redistribution of seats in the county of Hastings from any personal point of view at all. The committee dealing with this matter have dealt with me in the most generous spirit, in fact, thev have been generous to a fault. The riding of West Hastings, which I have

tbe honour to represent at a by-election returned me as their representative by a majority of over 500. That is a large" enough majority to satisfy any member, but by the action of the committee that majority, judging from the vote that was polled at "the last general election, will in all probability be increased to a majority somewhere between 1,200 and 1,500. Personally, I say, I am not complaining that the committee have given me such a favourable opportunity of representing West Hastings, but while I do not complain on my own behalf, I think I have a just right to complain of the manner in which my neighbours have been treated. The county of Hastings, as I view it, has two objections to make to the action of the committee. The first objection that occurs to me is that the committee have taken away altogether from the county of Hastings one member and have confined that county to a representation by two members. It appears to me that it is decidedly wrong and unjust to the county of Hastings as a whole. The matter has been pretty thoroughly discussed in connection with some other counties that have already been dealt with by this committee, and I shall not attempt to go over the reasons that have been pointed out why Hastings should have three representatives further than this:	The
county of Hastings has been represented by three members for a great number of years and in the redistribution which has taken place now it was found that by the distribution which the committee made some county in the province that would not strictly be entitled, according to the unit of population as laid down, to three members, must have that number of representatives. The county of Hastings did not have a population sufficient to entitle it to three members according to the strict letter of the law, but Hastings at the same time has enjoyed a representation of three members for many years past. What I complain of more particularly is, that, this being the state of affairs, Hastings have a population of upwards of 59,000, or very nearly 60,000, and having three representatives, that one of these representatives should be taken away while the county of Middlesex, which only has a population of 54,000, should be given an extra member. What justification is there for that ? If one county not coming right up to the strict letter of the law in regard to population to give it three members, is to enjoy that privilege when it has not the right to do so, why not allow a county which was enjoying that right to continue in the enjoyment of it instead of taking it away and giving additional ?-epre-sentation to the county of Middlesex, which has a smaller population than Hastings has ? That is all I desire to say upon that point. The second grievance that occurs to me is in regard to the division of Hastings. Taking it for granted that Hastings shall only have two members, it occurs to me that
in the division the committee have violated all the principles they have been advocating and that were laid down for their guidance and which they during the course of this debate in the committee have declared over and over again have governed and controlled their action in this matter. In the first place in regard to population, it has been stated by the right hon. leader of the government and also by members of the committee, that they have endeavoured as nearly as possible to equalize population so that there might be a fair representation of the people. Apply that principle to the county of Hastings. We have two ridings, and we find that in the riding of West Hastings there is a population of over 32,000, whereas in Bast Hastings there is a population of a little over 26,000, a difference of very nearly 6,000 in the population. Surely it cannot be contended in the face of that fact that the committee have been actuated in their conduct with a degire to make a fair distribution of population between the two ridings.

Ottawa, September, 12, 1903.
Sir,-While the difficulty in connection with the issuing of letters-of-credit exists I shall be very glad, as far as the working strength of the Audit Office will permit, to pass applications for Receiver General's cheques for the more pressing claims that are before your department. Dear Mr. Taylor,-The Minister of Finance is reported in this morning's ' Citizen ' as having said in reply to you that it was undoubtedly important that members should be able to draw a few dollars as the exhibition was on. This circular was written to remove as far as possible the dead-lock which until then I hoped from day to day would he shortly at an end.
At any time since the issuing of the circular the members could have been paid all their requirements, as they can now, within twenty-four hours, by applications for Receiver General's cheques from the clerk.
Will you oblige me by reading the circular and this letter to the House.
Yours sincerely,

This circular was written to remove as far as possible the deadlock which until then I hoped from day to day would shortly be at an end.
There seems to have been a deadlock between the Auditor General and the Finance Department, and he hoped from day to day that it would be removed. In reference to the statement made by my hon. friend from Haltou (Mr. Henderson), about bringing this matter up, I made one reference to it before to-day. The Auditor General has written to me as a member of the House, asking me to read this statement, and I have done so. I may say for myself that I have not drawn much of my indemnity; but only last Thursday, when I wanted to draw some, I was refused', and this week when I returned, the deadlock was still on. Several members have asked me if they could not get some money, and I thought it my duty to make reference to the matter. I do not care what impression goes to the country with reference to the members or the staff of the House. The law allows us so much indemnity for the session, and we can draw so much per diem if we need it. Many members have not drawn any yet, but the time has come when they'Feed some money, and why should we be inconvenienced when the country owes us the amount. It is no reflection on a member that he says he wants some mjoney and wants this deadlock to be brought to an end. If it is the fault of the Auditor General let us know it; if it is the fault of the Finance Minister, let us know it. He hoped from day to day that this deadlock would be brought to an end.

the hon. gentleman has not been able to receive his indemnity in the same way and with the same promptness as in the past is because the Auditor General has refused to issue to the Clerk of this House the usual letter of credit. I do not care what dispute he may have with other people, in my judgment he has no right to refuse that, and we propose to amend the law so that he shall not have the power to hold up members of the House or any department of the government on such a frivolous and unreasonable pretext. If the law authorizes him to take the stand he takes, the law should be amended.
